docs.title: gView.Pipe
docs.text: gView.Pipe is a workflow app: you connect nodes in an editor, and items flow from node to node. A workflow starts on a schedule, through a webhook, or by hand.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• User Guide: build, run and monitor workflows.
  • Admin Guide: install, configure and operate gView.Pipe.
  • Developer Guide: write your own nodes as plugins (English only).

docs.title: Admin Guide
docs.text:
This guide is for people who install and operate gView.Pipe.

  • Installation: ZIP and Docker, first start.
  • Configuration: settings, folders, environment variables.
  • Authentication: login with fixed users or an identity provider (OIDC).
  • Plugins: which plugins exist and how to install them.
  • Running scripts: release script folders and Git servers.
  • Operations: reverse proxy, webhooks, backup, updates, logs.
  • Security: what the app protects and what you must protect.
  • Troubleshooting: typical problems and their causes.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text: Scripts and CI pipelines use the REST API under /api/v1 to run workflows, look at executions and deploy workflows. The API has its own keys; it never uses the login of the UI.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Create keys on the page API keys (navigation). A key has:

Setting Meaning Name Who or what uses it, e.g. CI Deploy. Runs started with the key show API · CI Deploy in the history. Rights Read: workflows, executions, groups. Run: start, stop, replay runs. Deploy: create, change, delete, activate workflows. Portal: only the portal endpoints, for the user portal; use it alone. Only these groups Limits the key to the workflows of these groups. It doesn't see other workflows at all, also not workflows without a group. Expires After this day the key is refused. Empty: never.

The key (pipe_…) is shown once, when it is created. Only its SHA-256 is stored (data/api-keys.json), so a lost key can't be shown again: delete it and create a new one. The prefix pipe_ lets secret scanners, e.g. of GitHub, recognize keys that were committed by mistake.

Send the key as a header:

X-Pipe-Api-Key: pipe_…

or as Authorization: Bearer pipe_….

Warning

Only users with the role admin can create keys. With Pipe:Auth:Mode none everyone who can reach the UI is admin. Protect the UI with a login before you rely on keys. More than 60 failed attempts per minute from one address answer 429.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
The API is described in /api/v1/openapi.json (OpenAPI 3). Load it into a tool of your choice, e.g. Postman, Bruno or an OpenAPI viewer, to try the endpoints.

Method and path Right Does GET /api/v1/workflows read Lists the workflows. GET /api/v1/workflows/{id} read The workflow as JSON, with its version as ETag. PUT /api/v1/workflows/{id} deploy Creates or replaces the workflow (see below). DELETE /api/v1/workflows/{id} deploy Deletes the workflow. POST /api/v1/workflows/{id}/activate, /deactivate deploy Switches its triggers on or off. POST /api/v1/workflows/{id}/run run Starts a run (see below). GET /api/v1/executions read Executions, newest first. Filters: workflowId, status, mode, from, before, limit. GET /api/v1/executions/{workflowId}/{id} read One execution with the input, output and logs of each node. POST /api/v1/executions/{workflowId}/{id}/cancel run Stops a running or queued run. POST /api/v1/executions/{workflowId}/{id}/replay run Runs the execution again; body { "fromNodeId": "…" } to start at a node (Replay). GET /api/v1/groups read Lists the workflow groups. GET /api/v1/audit read The audit log, newest first. Filters: from, before, actor, area, objectId, limit. Only for keys that aren't limited to groups.

Errors are answered as application/problem+json with a title that says what is wrong.

docs.title: Running a workflow
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/workflows/{id}/run
{ "items": [ { "name": "Ada" } ], "environment": "TEST", "wait": true, "timeoutSeconds": 30 }

All fields are optional. The run starts at every node without an incoming connection, with items as their input (default: one empty item). It behaves like a triggered run: pinned data is ignored, the error workflow starts on failure and the queue of the workflow applies (Max queued runs).

Answer When 200 { executionId, status, error, errorNode, node, items } wait and the run ended in time; items is the output of the node that finished last. A failed run is also 200, with status: "error". 202 { executionId, status } Without wait, or the run takes longer than timeoutSeconds; ask GET /executions/{workflowId}/{executionId} later. 429 The workflow runs already and its queue is full.

docs.title: Deploying a workflow
docs.text:
PUT /api/v1/workflows/{id} takes the JSON of a workflow, as GET returns it or as stored in data/workflows. Before saving it is checked: unique node ids and names, connections between existing nodes, no cycles, installed node types, valid parameters. Problems answer 422 with a list in details.errors. Credentials that don't exist on this server are details.warnings in the answer, not errors.

Send If-Match with the ETag of a GET to make sure nobody changed the workflow in between; otherwise you get 412. Without If-Match the workflow is replaced. If the workflow is active, its triggers are armed again with the new version.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
curlPowerShell 
KEY=pipe_...
# run and wait for the result
curl -s -X POST https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/workflows/hello-pipe/run \
  -H "X-Pipe-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "items": [ { "name": "Ada" } ], "wait": true }'

# deploy a workflow from a file
curl -s -X PUT https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/workflows/hello-pipe \
  -H "X-Pipe-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary @hello-pipe.json

# the last failed runs
curl -s "https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/executions?status=error&limit=10" -H "X-Pipe-Api-Key: $KEY"

$headers = @{ "X-Pipe-Api-Key" = "pipe_..." }
# run and wait for the result
$body = @{ items = @(@{ name = "Ada" }); wait = $true } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/workflows/hello-pipe/run `
  -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body

# deploy a workflow from a file
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Put -Uri https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/workflows/hello-pipe `
  -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/json" -InFile hello-pipe.json

# the last failed runs
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/executions?status=error&limit=10" -Headers $headers

Credentials, variables and groups can't be changed through the API; set them up in the UI.

docs.title: Portal endpoints
docs.text:
For the user portal (users who run workflows, but don't edit them) a key with the right Portal reaches only /api/v1/portal. It cannot do anything else, and no other key reaches these endpoints. Every request names the user it is for in the header X-Pipe-On-Behalf-Of, and may list the portal roles of the user in X-Pipe-On-Behalf-Of-Roles (each role percent-encoded, separated by commas); runs show portal:<user> as the starter, and users see and stop only their own runs. The portal server is trusted to name the right user, so keep the key on that server and let only it reach the backend.

Method and path Does GET /api/v1/portal/workflows The published workflows with category, form and run settings. POST /api/v1/portal/workflows/{id}/run Starts a run. Body { "values": { … }, "mode": "wait" or "background" }. The values are checked against the form (422 with the fields that are wrong). Waiting answers with the result, or 202 when the wait timeout passed. GET /api/v1/portal/executions The runs of the user, newest first, with the running ones. GET /api/v1/portal/executions/{workflowId}/{id} Status and result of a run of the user. POST /api/v1/portal/executions/{workflowId}/{id}/cancel Stops a run of the user, unless the workflow forbids it.

Which workflows appear is set in the workflow settings: only workflows with Publish in portal are visible, in the category of their group. The Form Trigger declares the form, the Result node what the user sees at the end. Users never see raw items or error details of nodes: a failed run shows the Error message of the Result node, or a general text with the number of the run.

Each field of the form has a name, a type (text, multiline text, number, yes/no, date, choice, password), a label, a description, a placeholder, a default and Required. Text fields can have a pattern, a regular expression the text must match as a whole (e.g. [A-Z]{1,2}-\d{1,5}), with the message shown otherwise. The portal can check it while the user types; the backend checks it again on every start. Keep patterns to what .NET and JavaScript share.

Settings of the backend for the portal (section Pipe:Portal):

Setting Meaning MaxRunsPerUser Runs a user may have at the same time (default 3, 0 = no limit); more are answered with 429. HistoryDays Days the result and the entered values of a run are kept for the user (default 30, 0 = always); after that only the status is shown. NotifyWorkflowId The workflow that sends the mail when a run is done. Without it the portal offers no mail. PublicUrl The address of the portal, for the link in that mail.

GET /api/v1/portal/info tells the portal whether a mail can be sent (mailWhenDone) and the days kept (historyDays). notifyEmail in the body of a run asks for the mail.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
gView.Pipe has three login modes. You choose one per instance in _config/auth.config:

Mode Meaning none No login (default). Everyone who can reach the address may use the app. Use it only on localhost or a protected network. forms A login form with users from the configuration. oidc Login at an identity provider with OpenID Connect, for example IdentityServer.NET.

The login protects the user interface. Webhooks and the documentation under /docs stay reachable without a login; protect webhooks with a credential (see Security). Whoever is signed in may do everything.

docs.title: The file auth.config
docs.text:
On the first start the app creates _config/auth.config from the prototype _setup/proto/auth.config, next to pipe.config (see Configuration). Environment variables override it, for example Pipe__Auth__Mode=forms.

Setting Default Meaning Pipe:Auth:Mode none none, forms or oidc. Pipe:Auth:SessionMinutes 480 Minutes without a request until the login expires. Every request extends it. Pipe:Auth:UseForwardedHeaders false Trust the X-Forwarded-For/-Proto/-Host headers of a reverse proxy. Needed for OIDC behind a proxy that terminates https. Pipe:Auth:Users Users of the forms mode, see below. Pipe:Auth:LoginAttemptsPerMinute 10 Login attempts per minute and client address; more are answered with 429. Pipe:Auth:Oidc:* Settings of the oidc mode, see below.

docs.title: Forms: fixed users
docs.text:
{
  "Pipe": {
    "Auth": {
      "Mode": "forms",
      "Users": [
        { "Name": "admin", "PasswordHash": "pbkdf2-sha256$210000$..." },
        { "Name": "editor", "Password": "plain text" }
      ]
    }
  }
}

  • PasswordHash is preferred. Create it with the app itself:

    dotnet gView.Pipe.Shell.dll --hash-password "my password"

  • Password in plain text works too, but logs a warning on every start. If both are set, the hash counts.

  • Email (optional) is the address for mails to the user, e.g. when a run of the portal is done.
  • Email (optional) is the address for mails to the user, e.g. when a run of the portal is done.
  • User names are not case sensitive.
  • After a wrong password the app waits a second; the number of attempts per address is limited.

docs.title: Docker: the admin password as a variable
docs.text:
docker run -d --name gview-pipe -p 8080:8080 \
  -v gview-pipe-data:/app/data \
  -e PIPE_ADMIN_PASSWORD=change-me \
  ghcr.io/jugstalt/gview-pipe:latest

PIPE_ADMIN_PASSWORD sets the password of the user admin (another name with PIPE_ADMIN_USER). It replaces that user from auth.config, keeps the other users and switches the mode none to forms.

docs.title: OIDC: identity provider
docs.text:
{
  "Pipe": {
    "Auth": {
      "Mode": "oidc",
      "Oidc": {
        "Authority": "https://login.example.com",
        "ClientId": "gview-pipe",
        "ClientSecret": "secret",
        "Scopes": [ "openid", "profile", "role" ],
        "RoleClaimType": "role",
        "NameClaimType": "name",
        "RequiredRoles": [ "gview-pipe" ]
      }
    }
  }
}
Setting Default Meaning Authority Address of the identity provider. Required. ClientId Client id at the provider. Required. ClientSecret Secret of the client; leave it empty for a public client. In Docker: Pipe__Auth__Oidc__ClientSecret. Scopes openid profile role Requested scopes. RoleClaimType role Claim with the roles of the user. NameClaimType name Claim shown as the user name. RequiredRoles (empty) The user needs one of these roles. Empty: every user of the provider may enter. RequireHttpsMetadata true Set it to false only for a test provider without https.

The app uses the authorization code flow with PKCE. Register at the provider:

  • the redirect URI https://<app>/signin-oidc,
  • the post logout redirect URI https://<app>/signout-callback-oidc.

A user without one of the required roles sees a No access page with a Sign out button. Signing out also ends the session at the provider, so another account can sign in.

Behind a reverse proxy that terminates https, set UseForwardedHeaders to true, or the redirect URIs start with http:// (see Operations).

docs.title: Testing with the IdentityServer.NET of the AppHost
docs.text:
The AppHost starts IdentityServer.NET at https://localhost:8443 (ADD_IDENTITYSERVER, admin admin@is.net with the password admin) with the client local-gview-pipe/secret for https://localhost:7240. Windows must trust its self-signed certificate (import it into the user's trusted root certificates), or the browser and the app reject it. In its admin UI (https://localhost:8443/admin):

  1. Create the role gview-pipe (Roles).
  2. Create a user with this role and one without it (Users, then User Roles).
  3. Set Mode to oidc in _config/auth.config; the prototype already contains the settings of this client.

The user with the role can work; the other one sees No access.

The AppHost already creates users for this (password in brackets), all with the role gview-pipe: pipe-viewer@is.net (viewer), pipe-operator@is.net (operator), pipe-editor@is.net (editor) and pipe-admin@is.net (admin), and pipe-samples@is.net (samples), who is a viewer in general and an editor in the group Samples only. It also maps their roles (pipe-viewers, pipe-operators, pipe-editors, pipe-admins and pipe-samples-editors as editor@samples) to the roles of the Shell, so you only switch the mode on: uncomment #define PIPE_OIDC at the top of AppHost.cs (it sets Mode, the provider and the client for you, and a user needs the role gview-pipe). With #define PIPE_FORMS instead the Shell has fixed users without the IdentityServer: viewer, operator, editor, admin and samples, each with the name as password. Only one of the two may be defined. The settings reach the Shell as environment variables, which win over _config/auth.config; lists such as Users are merged by position, so move away a _config/auth.config of your own that has users. The user portal@is.net (portal) with the role portal-demo is for the portal.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
With a login, every user has a role. Each role may do what the ones before it may:

Role May viewer see workflows, executions and groups operator run, stop and replay workflows; activate and deactivate them editor create, change and delete workflows and groups; pin data admin credentials, the variables of the instance, API keys

viewer and operator open workflows read only: the editor shows Read only, without palette and Save; the fields can't be changed. Pages and buttons a role may not use are hidden or disabled. Without a login (Mode none) everyone is admin.

A user can have another role for the workflows of one group, e.g. viewer in general but editor in the group Billing. Credentials, instance variables and API keys only look at the role for the instance. Groups are named by their id (billing), as shown in the address of the group page.

Forms: per user in auth.config:

"Users": [
  { "Name": "admin", "PasswordHash": "…", "Role": "admin" },
  { "Name": "ada", "PasswordHash": "…", "Role": "viewer", "GroupRoles": { "billing": "editor" } }
]

OIDC: map values of the role claim (RoleClaimType) to roles; role@group gives the role for one group. The highest match wins, and a group never gets less than the role for the instance:

"Oidc": {
  "RoleMappings": {
    "pipe-admins": "admin",
    "pipe-operators": "operator",
    "pipe-billing": "editor@billing"
  }
}

Users without a role (a forms user without Role, an OIDC user without a mapped claim) get DefaultRole. Its default is admin, so an installation from before roles works as before. Once you have given the roles, set it to viewer:

"DefaultRole": "viewer"

The roles are worked out on every check from the configuration, not stored in the login: after changing auth.config and restarting the app they apply without signing in again. The account menu shows the own role, and with (+ groups) that there are others in some groups.

docs.title: Signing out
docs.text: With a login, the account icon at the top right shows the user name, the role and Sign out.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: gview-pipe is a command line client of the REST API for scripts and CI pipelines: deploy workflows from files, start runs and wait for them, look at executions.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dotnet tool install --global gView.Pipe.Cli
gview-pipe --help

This works once the package is published on NuGet. Until then build it from the source and install it from the folder:

dotnet pack src/gView.Pipe.Cli -c Release -o artifacts/cli
dotnet tool install --global gView.Pipe.Cli --add-source artifacts/cli

After a change, pack again and run dotnet tool update --global gView.Pipe.Cli --add-source artifacts/cli (raise the version in Directory.Build.props first, otherwise the cached package is used). dotnet tool uninstall --global gView.Pipe.Cli removes it.

It needs the .NET 10 runtime and an API key with the rights for what you do (read, run, deploy).

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
Set the address of the server and the key as environment variables, so the key doesn't appear in the process list or in logs of the pipeline:

bashPowerShell 
export PIPE_URL=https://pipe.example.com
export PIPE_API_KEY=pipe_...

$env:PIPE_URL = "https://pipe.example.com"
$env:PIPE_API_KEY = "pipe_..."

--url and --key do the same for one call.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Does gview-pipe workflows list [--json] Lists the workflows. gview-pipe workflows get <id> Prints the workflow as JSON. gview-pipe workflows export <id> --out <file or folder> Saves the workflow as a file; with a folder it is named <id>.json. gview-pipe workflows deploy <file or folder>... [--dry-run] [--force] Creates or replaces workflows from JSON files (folders: all *.json below). gview-pipe workflows delete <id> Deletes a workflow. gview-pipe workflows activate <id>, deactivate <id> Switches its triggers on or off. gview-pipe run <id> [--wait] [--input <file or ->] [--environment <name>] [--timeout <seconds>] [--json] Starts a run. gview-pipe executions list [--workflow <id>] [--status <status>] [--limit <n>] [--json] Lists executions, newest first. gview-pipe executions get <workflowId> <id> One execution with its node runs. gview-pipe executions cancel <workflowId> <id> Stops a running or queued run. gview-pipe executions replay <workflowId> <id> [--from <nodeId>] Runs an execution again.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
gview-pipe workflows deploy workflows/            # every *.json below the folder
gview-pipe workflows deploy hello-pipe.json --dry-run

The file is the JSON of a workflow, as gview-pipe workflows export writes it or as stored in data/workflows; the id inside names the workflow. The server checks it before saving; problems are listed and the exit code is 2.

  • A workflow that exists is only replaced if nobody changed it since the command read it, for example in the editor. Otherwise the command stops with a message; --force replaces it anyway.
  • --dry-run only reports would create or would update. It doesn't check the workflow; the server does that on the real deploy.
  • deploy never deletes. Remove workflows one by one with gview-pipe workflows delete.
  • Credentials that don't exist on the server are reported as warnings.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
gview-pipe run hello-pipe                                   # starts it, prints the execution id
gview-pipe run hello-pipe --wait --input item.json          # waits and prints the items of the last node
echo '{ "name": "Ada" }' | gview-pipe run hello-pipe --wait --input -

--input is a JSON object (one item) or an array of objects; - reads it from standard input. It starts like a triggered run, see Running a workflow.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Done. Without --wait a started run counts as done. 1 gview-pipe run --wait: the run ended with the status error. 2 Wrong call, or the server refused it (401 key, 404, 422 invalid workflow, 429 queue full).

A pipeline step can therefore use the command directly: a failed run or a refused deploy fails the step.

# example: GitHub Actions
- run: dotnet tool install --global gView.Pipe.Cli
- run: gview-pipe workflows deploy workflows/
  env:
    PIPE_URL: ${{ vars.PIPE_URL }}
    PIPE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PIPE_API_KEY }}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The settings are in _config/pipe.config in the working directory of the app (in the Pipe section, JSON with comments). If the file is missing at the start, the app creates it from the prototype _setup/proto/pipe.config; adjust it afterwards. appsettings.json holds only ASP.NET Core settings like Logging. Environment variables and the command line override pipe.config. The start scripts of the ZIP set the folders as environment variables.

The login has its own file _config/auth.config, created the same way from _setup/proto/auth.config (see Authentication).

In the Docker image /app/_config is a volume, so the files survive updates.

docs.title: Keeping the configuration over updates
docs.text: The variable PIPE_CONFIG_PATH moves the _config folder. The start scripts and gview-pipe-service.bat install set it to <root>\_config, next to the version folders, so every installation (root folder) has its own pipe.config and keeps it over updates. On the first start the app creates it there from the prototype. Edit <root>\_config\pipe.config; the version folder has no _config of its own.

docs.title: Settings
Environments and variables
docs.text:
Each instance runs in one environment: a test server in TEST, the production server in PROD. Groups and workflows inherit it unless they set their own, see Variables and environments. Users can't change the environment of the instance in the app.

{
  "Pipe": {
    "Environment": "PROD",
    "Environments": [ "TEST", "STAGE", "PROD" ],
    "Variables": {
      "DATABASE_SERVER": { "DEFAULT": "db-test", "PROD": "db-prod" },
      "DATABASE_PASSWORD": { "PROD": "..." }
    },
    "SecretVariables": [ "DATABASE_PASSWORD" ]
  }
}

Variables of the configuration are the lowest level. Values entered on the Variables page of the app win over them, per environment. The app stores those in variables.json in the data folder; secret values are encrypted with the keys in keys/. Secret values of groups and workflows are encrypted the same way, so a workflow file copied to another installation loses them.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Use two underscores for the nesting:

Pipe__DataPath=/var/lib/gview-pipe/data
Pipe__FileRoots__import=/srv/import
Pipe__Scripts__ScriptRoots__scripts=/srv/scripts
Pipe__Scripts__GitServers__company__Url=https://git.example.com
Pipe__Environment=PROD
Pipe__Variables__DATABASE_SERVER__PROD=db-prod

docs.title: Listening address
docs.text:
The start scripts listen on http://localhost:5100 by default. To change it, for example for a second instance on the same machine, set urls at the top of pipe.config (next to Pipe, not inside it):

{
  "urls": "http://localhost:5101",
  "Pipe": { ... }
}

urls in pipe.config wins over ASPNETCORE_URLS; --urls on the command line wins over both. The Windows service passes its port with --urls (gview-pipe-service.bat install <name> <port>). The Docker image uses http://*:8080.

docs.title: Limits that are not in the configuration
docs.text:
A few options can only be set in code (Program.cs of the Shell), for example how long a Wait node may wait (one hour), the JavaScript limits and the maximum body size of a webhook (10 MB). Ask your developer if you need to change them.

Per workflow you can set the maximum concurrent runs (default 1) in the workflow panel of the editor. More runs at the same time are skipped, and a webhook caller gets 429, unless Max queued runs lets triggered runs wait.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: gView.Pipe needs the .NET 10 runtime (ASP.NET Core). The Docker image brings its own.

docs.title: ZIP (Windows and Linux)
docs.text:
Download gview-pipe-win64-<version>.zip or gview-pipe-linux64-<version>.zip and unpack it into a folder of your choice, for example C:\gview-pipe. The ZIP contains one folder per version:

gview-pipe\
  0.1.0\
    pipe\                 the app and its plugins
    gview-pipe.bat        start script (gview-pipe.sh on Linux)
  data\                   created at the first start: workflows, executions, credentials, keys
  files\                  folder for Read File / Write File
  scripts\                folder for Run Script

data, files and scripts live next to the version folders, so they survive an update. The start script sets their location for you.

Start the app with the start script. It listens on http://localhost:5100. Open that address in a browser.

Note

The start script binds to localhost only. To reach the app from other machines, put a reverse proxy in front of it (see Operations) or set urls in <root>\_config\pipe.config (see Configuration). By default there is no login: switch one on before others can reach the app (see Authentication).

On the first start with an empty data folder, gView.Pipe copies the sample workflows into the group Samples.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
docker run -d --name gview-pipe -p 8080:8080 \
  -v gview-pipe-data:/app/data \
  ghcr.io/jugstalt/gview-pipe:latest
  • The app listens on port 8080 inside the container.
  • /app/data holds all runtime state: mount a volume or a folder, or the data is lost with the container.
  • The image contains git (for Run Scripts Repo) and python3 (for .py scripts). It has no PowerShell and no Windows shell, so .ps1, .bat and .cmd scripts don't run in it.
  • For Read File / Write File and script folders, mount the folders and name them in the configuration, for example -v /srv/pipe/files:/app/files -v /srv/pipe/scripts:/app/scripts. The defaults are files and scripts below /app.
  • For a login with the user admin, add -e PIPE_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<password> (see Authentication).

Settings are passed as environment variables, see Configuration.

docs.title: Starting automatically
docs.text:
The start script runs the app only as long as you are logged on. To keep it running on a server, run it as a Windows service, in IIS, as a systemd unit or in Docker. In every case, run it under an account with restricted rights, because scripts run with the rights of that account (see Security).

Active workflows with a Cron or Webhook trigger are armed again when the app starts.

docs.title: Windows service
docs.text:
The version folder contains gview-pipe-service.bat. Run it in a command prompt as administrator:

gview-pipe-service.bat install [name] [port]
gview-pipe-service.bat uninstall [name]

install creates the service and starts it:

  • Service name gview-pipe, or gview-pipe-<name> with a name. It starts automatically (delayed) and is restarted after a crash.
  • It listens on http://localhost:<port> (default 5100), like the start script.
  • It runs as the virtual account NT SERVICE\gview-pipe[-<name>], which may write only to data, files, scripts and _config.
  • data, files, scripts and _config next to the version folders are set as environment variables of the service, like in the start script.

Several instances on one server, for example production and test: unpack the ZIP into one root folder per instance and give each a name and a port.

D:\gview-pipe-prod\0.1.0\gview-pipe-service.bat install prod 5100
D:\gview-pipe-test\0.1.0\gview-pipe-service.bat install test 5200

install refuses a name whose service belongs to another root folder.

Update: unpack the new version into the same root folder and run its gview-pipe-service.bat install with the same name and port. The script stops the service, points it to the new version and starts it again. To go back, run install of the old version.

Own account: for network shares or Git with Windows authentication, the virtual account is not enough. Enter a domain or local account in the service properties (tab Log On) and give it write access to the same folders.

The log goes to the Windows event log (application log, source gView.Pipe, warnings and errors).

docs.title: IIS
docs.text:
gView.Pipe runs in IIS like any ASP.NET Core app:

  • Install the ASP.NET Core Hosting Bundle for .NET 10.
  • Create a site or application whose physical path is the pipe folder of the version.
  • Set the application pool to No Managed Code and give its identity write access to data, files, scripts and _config.

The start script does not run in IIS. Set PIPE_CONFIG_PATH=<root>\_config as an environment variable of the application pool (not in the web.config of the version, which an update replaces), and set the folders as absolute paths in <root>\_config\pipe.config (see Configuration).

docs.title: Linux and Docker
docs.text: Use a systemd unit that runs gview-pipe.sh or dotnet gView.Pipe.Shell.dll with the same environment variables, or a Docker restart policy (--restart unless-stopped).

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: The app serves this documentation itself under /docs (for example http://localhost:5100/docs), in the language of the browser (English or German). The Docs link in the top bar opens it. It works offline and always matches the installed version.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
• The start page opens and shows the sample workflows.
  • The log at the start says Plugins: <n> node types from <m> assemblies. If a plugin could not be loaded, a warning follows (see Troubleshooting).

docs.title: Running behind a reverse proxy
docs.text:
For access from other machines and for HTTPS, put a reverse proxy (IIS, nginx, Traefik, …) in front of the app. The app itself listens on plain HTTP.

  • Forward / to the app. The editor uses a live connection (Blazor Server, WebSockets): enable WebSocket forwarding and don't cut idle connections too early.
  • Webhooks are served under /webhook/<path>. If you want to expose only webhooks to the internet, forward just /webhook/ and keep the editor internal.
  • Without a login (Pipe:Auth:Mode = none), whoever can open the editor can create workflows and run everything you released. Switch on a login (see Authentication) or protect the editor with the proxy (authentication, IP restriction) or a VPN.
  • With the login mode oidc behind a proxy that terminates HTTPS, set Pipe:Auth:UseForwardedHeaders to true and let the proxy send X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host. Otherwise the app sends http:// redirect URIs to the identity provider, which rejects them.

docs.title: Webhooks in production
docs.text:
• Webhooks only work while the workflow is Active. After a restart, all active workflows are armed again.
  • A path belongs to exactly one workflow in the whole app. A second workflow with the same path can't be activated, and the editor shows the reason after saving.
  • Always set a credential (Basic Auth, Bearer Token or API Key Header) on webhooks that are reachable from outside. Without one, anyone who knows the URL can start the workflow.
  • The maximum body size is 10 MB (answer 413). Callers that wait for the workflow have a timeout per webhook (default 30 seconds). After it they get 202 and the run continues.
  • A workflow runs once at a time by default. More calls get 429 while it runs. Raise Max concurrent runs in the workflow panel if calls must run in parallel, or Max queued runs if they may wait. The queue is kept in memory: a restart drops waiting runs.
  • Runs are not canceled when the caller disconnects.

How callers see failures is described in Triggers and webhooks and Error handling.

docs.title: Execution history
docs.text:
The latest 50 executions per workflow are kept in data/executions/; Pipe:ExecutionRetention and Pipe:ExecutionRetentionDays (see Configuration) and the workflow panel change that. Switch off Save item data of executions in the workflow panel, and only statuses, counts and logs are stored. That is useful when items contain sensitive data.

Executions that are running live in the memory of the process. A restart ends them, and a Wait node that is waiting loses its run.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text:
The page Audit (admins only) shows who changed, deleted, ran or signed in, and when:

Area Recorded Workflow created, saved (with a summary: nodes added, removed and changed, connections, settings), deleted, activated, deactivated, moved, deployed through the API Group created, changed, deleted Credential created, changed, deleted; never the values Variables the instance variables changed; names only API key created, deleted Login signed in; failed sign-ins and refused API keys, at most one entry per minute and address, with the number of further attempts Execution started by hand or through the API, stopped, replayed

Triggered runs are not in the audit log; the execution history has them. Who is the user name, api:<key name> for the REST API, or anonymous without a login.

Filter by person, area, object id and time, and export what is shown as CSV (Export CSV). The workflow panel of the editor shows the last changes of the workflow under History. Scripts read the log with GET /api/v1/audit.

The entries are kept as one file of JSON lines per month in data/audit/ and deleted after Pipe:AuditRetentionDays (365, in whole months). Every entry is also written to the application log (category gView.Pipe.Audit). Who can write the data folder can change the files; if you need proof, keep the entries of a central log system.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
Back up the whole data folder, plus files and scripts if you use them:

Folder Content data/workflows/ One JSON file per workflow. Suitable for Git. data/groups.json Groups of the start page. data/credentials/ Credentials, encrypted. data/keys/ The keys that decrypt the credentials. data/executions/ History. Optional.

Important

Restore credentials/ and keys/ together. Without the keys, stored credentials can't be read, and you must enter them again.

Back up _config too (pipe.config, auth.config); it holds the settings and, in the login mode forms, the users. The keys in data/keys/ also protect the login cookies: new keys sign everybody out.

For a consistent copy, stop the app or copy while nothing is running. Files are written through a temporary file and then moved into place.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
ZIP: unpack the new version next to the old one, stop the old app, start the new start script. data, files and scripts stay where they are. Keep the old version folder until the new one works; to go back, start its script again.

Docker: pull the new image and recreate the container with the same volumes.

Nodes store the version of their parameters and are migrated automatically when an older workflow runs. Make a backup of data before an update anyway.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: The app logs to the console (and to the Aspire dashboard if you run it with Aspire). Look at the log for plugin warnings at the start and for node failures. The log level is set in the Logging section of appsettings.json.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
All nodes come from plugins. The built-in nodes (gView.Pipe.Plugins.dll) are always part of the app. Two further plugins are separate, because they bring their own dependencies or can run code:

Plugin Nodes Why separate gView.Pipe.Plugins.Database SQL SQL Server, PostgreSQL and SQLite drivers. gView.Pipe.Plugins.Office none; adds the format Excel to Extract from File and Convert to File The Excel library (MiniExcel). gView.Pipe.Plugins.Scripts Run Script, Run Scripts Folder, Run Scripts Repo Runs scripts on the server. Not installing it means no script execution.

The ZIP and the Docker image contain both. Remove a plugin folder to switch it off.

docs.title: Folder layout
docs.text:
Each plugin has its own folder below Pipe:PluginPath (default plugins). The main DLL must have the name of the folder:

pipe\
  plugins\
    gView.Pipe.Plugins.Database\
      gView.Pipe.Plugins.Database.dll
      (its dependencies)
    gView.Pipe.Plugins.Scripts\
      gView.Pipe.Plugins.Scripts.dll

A plugin is loaded into its own assembly context, so its dependencies don't clash with those of the app. Restart the app after adding or removing a plugin.

docs.title: Third-party plugins
docs.text: Copy the plugin folder into plugins\. Only install plugins from sources you trust: a plugin runs with the rights of the app and can do anything the app can do. How to write one is described in the Developer Guide.

docs.title: Workflows that use a missing plugin
docs.text: The workflow still opens and the node keeps its settings, but running it fails at that node with Unknown node type … Is the plugin installed?. Install the plugin and the workflow works again.

docs.title: User portal
docs.text:
The portal is a small web app for people who run workflows but don't edit them. They see the workflows released for them in categories, fill in a form, wait for the result or let the run go on in the background, and stop their own runs.

The portal is a separate app (gView.Pipe.Portal). It has no engine and no tools; it calls the portal endpoints of the backend (the normal gView.Pipe app) with an API key. It can run on another server, for example on the internet, while the backend stays in the internal network:

Browser  →  portal server  →  backend (REST API)

The key stays on the portal server. The browser never talks to the backend and never sees the key.

docs.title: Set up the backend
docs.text:
1. On the page API keys create a key with the right Portal only. Copy it; it is shown once.
  2. Let only the portal server reach the backend (a VPN, a firewall rule or a private network). A stolen key could otherwise act as any user.
  3. Release workflows: in the workflow settings switch on Publish in portal. The group of the workflow is its category in the portal. Add a Form Trigger for the inputs and a Result node for what the user should see at the end.

docs.title: Configure the portal
docs.text:
Settings are read from appsettings.json, from portal.config.json next to the app and from the environment (Portal__BackendUrl).

Setting Meaning Portal:BackendUrl Address of the backend, e.g. https://pipe.internal:7240. Needed. Portal:ApiKey The key with the right Portal. Needed. Prefer the environment variable Portal__ApiKey. Portal:Title Name in the title bar (default gView.Pipe). Portal:PollSeconds Seconds between two status requests while a run goes on (default 2). Portal:Auth The login of the users, the same settings as Pipe:Auth: Mode is None, Forms or Oidc.

Warning

With Mode None everybody who reaches the portal is the user anonymous and sees the runs of all anonymous users. Use a login whenever the portal can be reached by more than you.

The name of the signed-in user goes to the backend with every request. Runs show portal:<name> as the starter in the history of the editor, and users see and stop only their own runs.

Start it like the Shell: dotnet run --project src/gView.Pipe.Portal (port 5250 in development, --launch-profile https for https on 7250). In the AppHost the login is set at the top of AppHost.cs: #define PORTAL_OIDC (IdentityServer, user portal@is.net) or #define PORTAL_FORMS (fixed users portal, with the portal role portal-demo and an address, and guest, both with the name as password); define only one.

For the forms mode create the hash of a password with the portal itself:

dotnet gView.Pipe.Portal.dll --hash-password "my password"

and put it into PasswordHash of the user (see Authentication). With OpenID Connect the client of the portal needs the redirect URIs <portal address>/signin-oidc and <portal address>/signout-callback-oidc. The portal needs https for it, behind a proxy with Portal:Auth:UseForwardedHeaders. It asks for the scopes openid profile role email unless you set Portal:Auth:Oidc:Scopes; email brings the address for the mail when a run is done, so the client must be allowed this scope.

docs.title: What users can do
docs.text:
• Workflows: all published workflows by category, with a search.
  • Form: the fields of the Form Trigger. Fields with a pattern are checked while the user types; the backend checks every start again.
  • Wait or background: the author sets the default and whether users may switch. A run the user waits for goes on in the background when the wait timeout has passed.
  • My runs: the runs of the user with their status. Running runs have a Stop button, unless the workflow forbids it. Finished runs have Run again, which opens the form with the values of that run (passwords are never kept).
  • Result: text, Markdown (without raw HTML) or a table, as defined by the Result node. Users never see raw items or the details of errors.

docs.title: Who sees which workflows
docs.text:
Without further settings every signed-in user sees all published workflows. To show some of them to some people only, use portal roles:

  1. Give the users roles at the login of the portal. With OpenID Connect these are the claims of the role claim type of the provider (Portal:Auth:Oidc:RoleClaimType, default role). In the forms mode add Roles to the users in Portal:Auth:Users:

    { "Name": "ada", "PasswordHash": "…", "Roles": [ "hr", "finance" ] }
    2. In the editor name the roles that may see a workflow (Only these roles in its portal settings) or all published workflows of a group (Portal roles in the group dialog). The roles of a workflow count before those of its group. Without roles everybody sees it.

A user needs one of the roles; case is ignored. A workflow the roles don't allow is not listed, can't be started and its runs aren't shown. These roles are not the roles viewer to admin of the editor, and they are checked by the backend, not by the portal. Roles come from the login, so a change applies at the next sign-in.

docs.title: Mail when a run is done
docs.text:
A user can tick Mail me when it is done when starting a run. The mail is sent by a workflow that you build, so you decide its text and its SMTP server:

  1. Create a workflow with an Execute Workflow Trigger and a Send Email node, e.g. portal-mail. The trigger gives it one item:

    {
  "to": "ada@example.com",
  "user": "ada",
  "workflow": { "id": "invoice", "name": "Invoice" },
  "execution": { "id": "…", "status": "success", "startedAt": "…", "finishedAt": "…", "url": "https://portal.example.com/jobs/invoice/…" }
}

    In the Send Email node use {{ $json.to }} as recipient, and for the text e.g. Your run of {{ $json.workflow.name }} ended: {{ $json.execution.status }}. {{ $json.execution.url }}. The item never holds the result of the run. 2. On the backend set Pipe:Portal:NotifyWorkflowId to its id, and Pipe:Portal:PublicUrl to the address of the portal, so url is filled.

The option appears only when the backend has a notification workflow and the user has an address: from the login (OIDC claim email) or, in the forms mode, the Email of the user in Portal:Auth:Users (the settings of the portal, not of the backend). No mail is sent when the user already got the result while waiting. A run that is still going when the backend restarts doesn't send its mail.

docs.title: Results and history
docs.text: Users see their own runs with the values they entered and the result for Pipe:Portal:HistoryDays days (default 30); after that only the status. Values of password fields are not shown. The history of the editor keeps the data of the run as usual, so switch off Save item data of executions for workflows with secrets.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: A user may have Pipe:Portal:MaxRunsPerUser runs at the same time on the backend (default 3), and a workflow can allow only one run at a time. Beyond that the portal shows the message of the backend.

docs.title: Running scripts
docs.text: The script nodes run existing scripts (.bat, .cmd, .ps1, .py, .sh) from workflows. Running code on the server is risky by nature, so you decide what may run: workflows can't type in a path or a command. They can only pick files from sources you release.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install the plugin gView.Pipe.Plugins.Scripts (see Plugins). Without it, the nodes don't exist.

The interpreter is chosen by the file extension. Only what the operating system can run is available:

Extension Interpreter .bat, .cmd cmd.exe (Windows) .ps1 pwsh, otherwise Windows PowerShell .py python .sh bash

Change an interpreter with Pipe:Scripts:Interpreters, for example ".py": "C:\\Python313\\python.exe".

docs.title: Script folders
docs.text:
A script folder is a folder on the server that you release by name:

"Pipe": {
  "Scripts": {
    "ScriptRoots": { "scripts": "D:\\ops\\scripts", "maintenance": "D:\\ops\\maintenance" }
  }
}

The nodes Run Script and Run Scripts Folder list the files of these folders, including subfolders.

Warning

Keep script folders apart from the folders you release for Write File (Pipe:FileRoots). Otherwise a workflow could write a script and then run it.

docs.title: Git servers
docs.text:
Run Scripts Repo takes scripts from a repository of a Git server you configure. Gitea and GitHub are supported:

"Pipe": {
  "Scripts": {
    "GitServers": {
      "company": {
        "Provider": "gitea",
        "Url": "https://git.example.com",
        "Owner": "ops",
        "CredentialId": "git-token",
        "RepositoryFilter": "^ops-"
      }
    }
  }
}
Setting Meaning Provider gitea or github. Decides which API lists repositories, branches and files. Url Base URL, for example https://github.com. Owner The organization or user whose repositories are offered. CredentialId The id of a Pipe credential (Basic Auth with user and password or token, or Bearer Token). Create it in the credentials list first. RepositoryFilter Optional regular expression; only repositories whose name matches are offered.

Each run makes a shallow clone (git clone --depth 1) into a temporary folder below Pipe:Scripts:RepositoriesPath, runs the scripts there and deletes the folder afterwards, also after a failure or cancel. Leftovers are removed when the app starts. There is never a stale checkout. The credential reaches git as an HTTP header in the environment, never in the URL or in a log. Only HTTPS (or local paths) works, no SSH.

The git command line must be installed on the server (it is part of the Docker image).

docs.title: How a script runs
docs.text:
• One process per script, with the script's folder (the repository root for Run Scripts Repo) as working directory.
  • The environment contains the environment of the app plus PIPE_ITEM, PIPE_WORKFLOW, PIPE_EXECUTION, PIPE_ENVIRONMENT, the variables of workflow, group and instance, the variables of the node (which override them) and, if the node has a credential, PIPE_CREDENTIAL_<FIELD>. Credential values and secret variables are masked in the output and in logs.
  • The default timeout is 10 minutes per script. A timeout or a cancel ends the whole process tree.
  • The output is limited to 1 MB per stream and is also written to the log of the node.
  • A script fails when its exit code is not 0, or when a line of its output matches the error pattern of the node (a regular expression).

How a failing script affects the workflow is described in Error handling.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Scripts run with the rights of the app's account. Run the app under an account that may do only what the scripts need. See Security.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: This page lists what the app protects and what you must protect yourself.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
Without configuration (Pipe:Auth:Mode = none), the editor and all its functions are open to everyone who can reach the address. Then:

  • bind the app to localhost or an internal network, and
  • put a reverse proxy or a VPN in front of it if people connect from other machines.

As soon as other people can reach the app, switch on a login: fixed users (forms) or an identity provider (oidc), see Authentication. Everyone who is signed in may do everything; there are no roles inside the app. Serve the app over https when it has a login, so passwords and the session cookie are encrypted.

docs.title: What a workflow can do
docs.text:
A workflow can call web addresses (HTTP Request), send mail, read and write files, run SQL and, with the script plugin, run scripts. You limit that by what you release:

Capability Limited by Read File / Write File Only the folders in Pipe:FileRoots, addressed by name. Scripts Only files from Pipe:Scripts:ScriptRoots or from the configured Git servers. No inline scripts, no free paths. SQL Only through a Connection String credential. Values are always parameters; the SQL text is never evaluated as an expression. JavaScript (expressions, Code node) A sandboxed engine with time and memory limits.

Whoever can edit workflows can use everything you release. Treat editor access as administrator access to the released folders, servers and credentials.

docs.title: Scripts run with the account of the app
docs.text: Run the app under an account (or container) that may do only what your scripts need. Don't run it as an administrator or root.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
• Credentials are stored encrypted with ASP.NET Data Protection. Secret fields are never shown again after saving.
  • Nodes reference credentials by id. They are not part of the workflow JSON, so you can share workflow files.
  • The keys are stored in data/keys/. Anyone with access to both keys/ and credentials/ can decrypt the credentials. Restrict access to the data folder. For production, a developer can configure Data Protection to protect the keys with DPAPI, a certificate or a key vault.
  • The headers authorization, proxy-authorization and cookie of webhook calls (and the API key header) are not copied into the items and so never reach the execution history. Credential values are masked in script output and logs.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text: Give every webhook that is reachable from outside a credential. See Operations.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
The REST API under /api/v1 accepts only API keys, never the login cookie of the UI.

  • Give each script or pipeline its own key with only the rights it needs, limited to its groups and with an expiry date. Delete keys that are no longer used; the page shows when each was last used.
  • Only the SHA-256 of a key is stored in data/api-keys.json; a copy of the data folder doesn't reveal keys.
  • Only admins create keys (roles). Without a login everyone is admin: use one when the UI is reachable by others.
  • Send keys only over HTTPS.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text: A plugin runs with the full rights of the app. Install only plugins from sources you trust.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text: The audit log records who changed, deleted or ran what, sign-ins and refused attempts. It never contains values of credentials or secret variables. For proof that can't be changed afterwards, forward the application log (category gView.Pipe.Audit) to a central log system.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text: Install updates regularly. The runtime and the third-party libraries receive security fixes.

docs.title: The app doesn't start
docs.text:
• Port in use: another program uses the port. Change it with --urls.
  • Missing runtime: dotnet gView.Pipe.Shell.dll needs the .NET 10 ASP.NET Core runtime (not needed for Docker).
  • No write access: the account needs write access to the data folder.

docs.title: A node is missing in the palette
docs.text:
The plugin isn't installed or couldn't be loaded. Check:

  1. The folder is plugins/<Name>/ and contains <Name>.dll with exactly the folder's name.
  2. The log at the start. A plugin that can't be loaded gives a warning that starts with Plugins:.
  3. You restarted the app after copying the plugin.

docs.title: Script nodes don't run a script
docs.text:
• The script isn't in a released folder, or the folder isn't in Pipe:Scripts:ScriptRoots.
  • The interpreter isn't installed (python, pwsh, bash). Set the path in Pipe:Scripts:Interpreters.
  • Run Scripts Repo: git isn't installed, the Git server or its credential is wrong, or the repository filter hides the repository. The node shows hints about missing settings.
  • In Docker: .ps1, .bat and .cmd scripts can't run in the Linux image.
  • The node reports failed although the script looks fine: a non-zero exit code or a line that matches the error pattern fails it. Look at the log of the node for the output of the script.

docs.title: A webhook answers with an error
docs.text:
Answer Cause 404 The workflow isn't active, or the path is wrong. Webhook paths are lower case. 405 The method differs from the one set in the trigger. 401 The credential is missing or wrong. 413 The body is larger than 10 MB. 429 The workflow is already running, its limit of concurrent runs is reached and no room is left in its queue. 503 The run waited in the queue longer than the webhook's timeout. Retry later, or raise the timeout or Max concurrent runs. 500 The run failed. The body has the error and the executionId; look the run up in the history. See Error handling.

If a workflow can't be activated because its path is already used, the editor shows which workflow and node use it.

docs.title: Credentials stopped working after a move or restore
docs.text: The data/keys/ folder doesn't match data/credentials/. Restore both from the same backup, or enter the credentials again.

docs.title: A workflow stops after a restart
docs.text: Runs that were in progress end with a restart. Active workflows are armed again, but a Wait node that was waiting has lost its run.

docs.title: Nobody can sign in
docs.text:
• Forms: the log says that no users are configured, or the user has neither Password nor PasswordHash. User names ignore case, passwords don't. After 10 attempts per minute from one address the app answers 429; wait a minute.
  • OIDC, the app doesn't start: Pipe:Auth:Oidc needs Authority and ClientId.
  • OIDC, an error at the identity provider about the redirect URI: register https://<app>/signin-oidc and https://<app>/signout-callback-oidc at the client. Behind a reverse proxy see Operations.
  • OIDC, a certificate error in the log: the app must trust the certificate of the provider. A self-signed test certificate must be imported into the trusted root certificates.
  • No access although the user has the role: the role must reach the app in the claim RoleClaimType (default role). Request the scope role and check that the provider puts the roles into the token or userinfo.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
• The application log (console, service log or docker logs).
  • The execution history of the workflow: each node shows its input, output and log.

docs.title: Developer Guide
docs.text:
This guide is for people who extend gView.Pipe with their own nodes and credential types, or embed it in another app. It is available in English only.

  • Writing a node: the contract, a first node, ports, triggers, errors.
  • Parameters and the editor form: how a parameter class becomes a form.
  • Plugins: packaging, loading, services and credential types.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
Project Purpose gView.Pipe.Abstraction The plugin SDK: contracts, attributes and models. No UI dependencies, and it stays small: plugins share it with the host. gView.Pipe.Core The headless engine: plugin catalog and loader, expression evaluator, scheduler, trigger manager, stores. gView.Pipe.AspNetCore ASP.NET Core integration: app.MapPipeWebhooks(). The only place with HTTP types. gView.Pipe.Plugins The built-in nodes and credential types. They use only the Abstraction, exactly like external plugins. gView.Pipe.Plugins.Database, .Scripts External plugins with their own dependencies, examples for plugin code. gView.Pipe.Razor MudBlazor components: workflow list, credential list and the editor. They depend on the Abstraction only. gView.Pipe.Shell The app itself: layout, routing and service composition.

The decisions behind the design are recorded in docs/adr in the repository.

docs.title: How a run works
docs.text:
1. A trigger (manual, cron, webhook, another workflow or an error) starts an execution with one or more items.
  2. The engine walks the graph, which is a DAG without cycles. A node starts when all the nodes it depends on have finished. Independent branches run in parallel.
  3. A node gets all items of its inputs, returns items per output port, and the engine hands them to the next nodes. Nodes whose inputs are all empty are skipped.
  4. Each node run records its input, output and log. Failures follow the node's error setting (stop, continue, error output).

Items are JSON objects plus optional binary attachments. Nodes need no knowledge of the engine, only of IPipeNodeContext.

docs.title: Embedding in another Blazor app
docs.text:
builder.Services
    .AddPipeCore()
    .AddPipeFileStore(options => options.RootPath = "data")
    .AddPipeRazor();

// ...
app.MapPipeWebhooks();

The host references the MudBlazor and Z.Blazor.Diagrams CSS and JavaScript plus _content/gView.Pipe.Razor/css/gview-pipe.css, and renders the components interactively without prerendering. Navigation is the host's job: the components raise events such as OnOpen and OnClose. See App.razor of the Shell.

AddPipeCore() alone registers in-memory stores, which is what tests use. AddPipeFileStore() stores workflows, groups, executions and credentials as JSON files.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Namespaces mirror folders and use file-scoped declarations. Public types are prefixed with Pipe.
  • JSON is camelCase, enums are camelCase strings. Always use PipeJson.Options so the engine, the UI and plugins bind parameters the same way.
  • Node and credential ids are GUIDs that never change once published: workflows store them.
  • Code, comments and UI text are in English.

docs.title: Parameters and the editor form
docs.text:
The editor builds the form of a node from its parameter class. It shows every public property with a getter and setter, in order. Attributes only refine how a property looks. The same class is filled from the stored JSON when the node runs.

public sealed class SendThingParameters
{
    [Required, PipeParameter(Label = "Url", Order = 1, Placeholder = "https://example.com/api")]
    public string Url { get; set; } = "";

    [PipeParameter(Label = "Method", Order = 2, Expressions = false)]
    public ThingMethod Method { get; set; } = ThingMethod.Post;

    [PipeParameter(Label = "Headers", Order = 3, Description = "Request headers")]
    public Dictionary<string, string> Headers { get; set; } = new();

    [PipeCredential(PipeBuiltInCredentials.BearerToken)]
    [PipeParameter(Label = "Credential", Expressions = false)]
    public string? CredentialId { get; set; }
}

docs.title: [PipeParameter]
docs.text: Property Effect Label The field label. Without it the property name is split into words (StopOnFirstFailure → "Stop on first failure"). Description Helper text under the field, and the description in the generated node reference. Placeholder Example text in an empty field. Order Position in the form. Properties without an order follow in declaration order. Multiline A larger text field. Expressions Whether the field offers {{ }} expressions (default true for text and JSON). Switch it off for fixed values such as modes and paths of configuration. Code Source code: a large monospace field, never evaluated as an expression. Read such values from context.RawParameters.

docs.title: Types and fields
docs.text:
C# type Field string Text field. bool Switch. int, long, double, decimal Number field. enum Selection of the values, stored as camelCase text (WhenFinished → whenFinished). JsonNode? A field that accepts text, numbers or JSON, with expressions. Dictionary<string, string> A list of name/value pairs. List<string> A list of values. List<PipeSelection> with [PipeOptions] An ordered list of options that can be switched on and off.

[Required] (DataAnnotations) marks a field as required in the form and in the node reference.

docs.title: Other attributes
docs.text: Attribute Use [PipeCredential(typeIds…)] on a string? The field is a drop-down with the stored credentials of those types. It holds the credential's id. [PipeWorkflowReference] on a string? A workflow picker. It holds the workflow's id. [PipeOptions] Values computed by the server (IPipeParameterOptions). [Secret] (credential classes) The field is masked and never shown again.

docs.title: Names in JSON
docs.text: Parameters are stored as camelCase JSON (CredentialId → credentialId) with enums as camelCase strings. Always use PipeJson.Options from gView.Pipe.Abstraction.Serialization when you serialize or deserialize parameters yourself, so you bind exactly like the engine and the editor.

docs.title: Node reference
docs.text: The user documentation lists every node with its parameters, generated from these attributes: dotnet run --project src/gView.Pipe.Docs. Write Description texts for the people who read that page: what the field does, its unit and what happens when it is empty.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text: Built-in nodes and external nodes use the same mechanism: assemblies are scanned for [PipeNode] and [PipeCredentialType] classes.

docs.title: An external plugin project
docs.text:
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <CopyLocalLockFileAssemblies>true</CopyLocalLockFileAssemblies>
    <EnableDynamicLoading>true</EnableDynamicLoading>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the contracts come from the host: never ship them with the plugin -->
    <PackageReference Include="gView.Pipe.Abstraction" Version="…" ExcludeAssets="runtime" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

gView.Pipe.Plugins.Scripts and gView.Pipe.Plugins.Database in the repository are complete examples. They use a project reference with Private="false" ExcludeAssets="runtime".

Build, then copy the output into plugins/<Name>/ of the app, where <Name> is the name of the main assembly:

plugins\
  MyCompany.PipeNodes\
    MyCompany.PipeNodes.dll
    (dependencies, native libraries)

docs.title: How plugins are loaded
docs.text:
• The app folder is scanned for gView.Pipe.Plugins*.dll (the built-in nodes). Pipe:PluginPath is scanned for plugin folders.
  • Each plugin folder is loaded into its own AssemblyLoadContext, with its dependencies resolved from its deps.json. Plugins may use different versions of a library without conflicts.
  • Assemblies named gView.Pipe.Abstraction, Microsoft.Extensions.*, Microsoft.AspNetCore.* and System.* always come from the host, so the plugin and the host share the same types. Don't ship them.
  • Plugins are loaded when the host configures its services, so they can register services before the container is built. Plugins can't be unloaded: restart the app after an update.
  • A problem while loading gives a warning in the log that starts with Plugins:, and the plugin is skipped. An id used by two classes keeps the first and warns.

Workflows that use a node of a plugin that isn't installed still load, and the node's data is kept. Running such a node fails with "Unknown node type".

docs.title: Services and options
docs.text:
Implement IPipePluginStartup (public, parameterless constructor) to register services:

public sealed class MyPluginStartup : IPipePluginStartup
{
    public void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services)
    {
        services.AddOptions<MyOptions>().Configure<IServiceProvider>((options, provider) =>
        {
            if (provider.GetService<IConfiguration>() is { } configuration)
            {
                configuration.GetSection("Pipe:MyPlugin").Bind(options);
            }
        });
        services.AddHttpClient("my-plugin");
    }
}

Nodes get services through their constructor. Settings an administrator controls (released folders, servers) belong in options like this, never in a node parameter: that way a workflow can't widen what it is allowed to do.

docs.title: Credential types
docs.text:
A credential type is a POCO with [PipeCredentialType]; its properties are the fields of the form:

[PipeCredentialType("5b7f3c2a-1d4e-4f7a-9c0b-2a6d8e1f3b45", "My Service", Description = "Token and URL of My Service")]
public sealed class MyServiceCredential
{
    [Required, PipeParameter(Label = "Base URL")]
    public string Url { get; set; } = "";

    [Required, Secret, PipeParameter(Label = "Token")]
    public string Token { get; set; } = "";
}

A node references it with [PipeCredential("5b7f3c2a-…")] on a string? parameter and reads it with await context.GetCredentialAsync<MyServiceCredential>(parameters.CredentialId). Never log secret values and never copy them into items: items end up in the execution history.

docs.title: Rules for ids
docs.text:
• The GUID of a node or credential type is its identity in stored workflows. Never change it, and don't reuse it.
  • Built-in ids are listed in PipeBuiltIn.cs of gView.Pipe.Plugins.
  • When a node's parameters change incompatibly, increase Version and add an IPipeNodeMigration instead of a new id.

docs.title: Writing a node
docs.text: A node is a class that implements IPipeNode<TParameters> and carries a [PipeNode] attribute. Reference gView.Pipe.Abstraction only.

docs.title: A first node
docs.text:
using gView.Pipe.Abstraction.Data;
using gView.Pipe.Abstraction.Nodes;

namespace MyCompany.PipeNodes;

public sealed class ShoutNodeParameters
{
    [PipeParameter(Label = "Field", Description = "The text field to turn to upper case")]
    public string Field { get; set; } = "name";
}

[PipeNode("9d6c1c3e-6a60-4b3a-9c43-0f6b6a6f2b11", "Shout",
    Category = "Transform",
    Description = "Turns a text field of each item to upper case.")]
public sealed class ShoutNode : PipeItemNodeBase<ShoutNodeParameters>
{
    protected override Task<PipeItem?> ProcessItemAsync(
        PipeItem item, ShoutNodeParameters parameters, IPipeNodeContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        if (item.Json[parameters.Field]?.GetValue<string>() is { } text)
        {
            item.Json[parameters.Field] = text.ToUpperInvariant();
        }

        return Task.FromResult<PipeItem?>(item);   // null drops the item
    }
}
  1. The attribute. [PipeNode("<guid>", "Name")] registers the class. Create a new GUID for every node and never change it: workflows store the id, not the class name, so you may rename and move classes freely. Category decides the palette group, Description the tooltip and the node reference.
  2. The parameters. A class with a parameterless constructor. The editor generates the form from its public properties (Parameters and the editor form).
  3. The logic. PipeItemNodeBase<T> calls ProcessItemAsync for every item, with the parameters already evaluated for that item ({{ }} expressions resolved). For anything else implement IPipeNode<T> yourself:
public Task<PipeNodeResult> ExecuteAsync(IPipeNodeContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    var items = context.GetInput();                       // all items of the main input
    var parameters = context.GetParameters<MyParameters>(items.FirstOrDefault());
    // ...
    return Task.FromResult(PipeNodeResult.FromMain(result));
}

A new instance of the class is created for every execution and constructor injection works, so don't keep state between runs. Services come from the application's container (plugins can add their own, see Plugins).

docs.title: The context
docs.text:
IPipeNodeContext is everything a node needs:

Member Purpose GetInput(port) The items that arrived on an input port (default main). GetParameters<T>(item, index) The parameters with all {{ }} expressions evaluated against item. RawParameters The stored parameters, expressions not evaluated. Evaluate(template, item) Evaluates a template string such as "Hello {{ $json.name }}". GetCredentialAsync<T>(id) The decrypted data of a credential, bound to your credential class. Logger Writes to the application log and to the node's Logs tab. BinaryStore Reads and writes the bytes of binary attachments. ExecuteWorkflowAsync(id, items) Runs another workflow as a sub-workflow. Environment, Variables The environment of the run and its resolved variables. Mask Variables.SecretValues in anything the node outputs. WorkflowId, WorkflowName, ExecutionId, NodeId, NodeName Where you are. Services The services of the current execution scope.

docs.title: Items
docs.text: A PipeItem is a JsonObject (item.Json) plus Binary, a dictionary of attachment references by name. The engine clones items on their way into a node, so changing them doesn't affect other branches. To produce a new item, build a new PipeItem(new JsonObject { ... }). Keep Binary when the item still stands for the same file.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
By default a node has one input and one output, main. Declare others on the attribute:

[PipeNode("…", "Split by Size", Outputs = new[] { "small", "large" })]

and return the items per port:

return PipeNodeResult.FromPorts(("small", small), ("large", large));

A port that gets no items stays empty, and nodes behind it are skipped. If the number of ports depends on the parameters (like Switch), implement IPipeDynamicPorts: GetInputs and GetOutputs receive the stored parameters and return the ports. Nodes with the error mode Route items to an error output get an extra error port from the engine.

docs.title: Expressions in code
docs.text:
Parameters are evaluated for you. To run JavaScript from a node (a Code-like node), inject IPipeScriptRunner:

var scope = context.CreateExpressionScope(item, index);
var result = _scripts.Run(code, scope, log: line => context.Logger.LogInformation("{Line}", line), cancellationToken: cancellationToken);

Don't reference the JavaScript engine (Jint) from plugins. A code field must not be evaluated as an expression: mark it [PipeParameter(Code = true)] and read it from context.RawParameters, because GetParameters evaluates {{ }} in every string.

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text:
A trigger starts executions. Implement IPipeTriggerNode next to IPipeNode<T>:

public Task<IAsyncDisposable?> ActivateAsync(IPipeTriggerContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    var parameters = context.GetParameters<MyTriggerParameters>();
    var registration = context.Host.RegisterSchedule("*/5 * * * *", TimeZoneInfo.Utc,
        ct => context.FireAsync([new PipeItem()], ct));
    // registration is an IDisposable that removes the schedule; wrap it in an IAsyncDisposable
    return Task.FromResult<IAsyncDisposable?>(new Handle(registration));
}
  • ActivateAsync is called when an active workflow is saved or the app starts. Return a handle that disarms the trigger.
  • context.Host offers RegisterSchedule (cron) and RegisterWebhook (HTTP, served by MapPipeWebhooks()).
  • FireAsync starts an execution at this trigger and completes when it has finished. It returns null when the workflow's limit of concurrent runs skipped the run, or when it left the queue. Pass a PipeQueueTicket in PipeTriggerFireOptions to learn whether the run started, waits or was skipped, and to take it out of the queue with TryAbandon (see the Webhook Trigger).
  • ExecuteAsync of a trigger usually just passes the trigger items on: PipeNodeResult.FromMain(context.GetInput()).
  • IPipeSubWorkflowTrigger and IPipeErrorTrigger are markers for the entry points of sub-workflows and error workflows.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• Throw PipeException for expected problems with a message the user can act on ("Select a connection"). The message appears on the node.
  • Throw PipeNodeException(message, items) when you have result items worth keeping even though the node failed (for example the output of scripts that ran). With the error mode Continue or Error output the engine passes those items on instead of the input items.
  • Respect cancellationToken; the user can stop a run.
  • Retries and timeouts are done by the engine according to the node's settings.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text: IPipeNodeHints.GetHints(parameters) returns notes the editor shows above the parameters, for example the URL of a webhook or a warning about a missing credential.

docs.title: Changing parameters later
docs.text: Increase Version on the attribute when you rename or restructure parameters, and implement IPipeNodeMigration. The engine calls MigrateParameters(fromVersion, parameters) before running a node whose workflow was saved with an older typeVersion.

docs.title: Values that depend on the server
docs.text: A parameter can offer values that the server computes from the other parameters (for example the files of a folder): mark it with [PipeOptions] and implement IPipeParameterOptions on the node. A string becomes a choice of one option, a List<PipeSelection> an ordered list whose entries can be switched on and off. Refreshable = true adds a refresh button.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: src/tests/gView.Pipe.Plugins.Tests/PluginTestHost.cs builds a host with the built-in nodes, in memory, and runs workflows. Use the same approach for your plugin: register your assembly in PipeCoreOptions.PluginAssemblies and run a workflow made with the PipeWorkflowBuilder of gView.Pipe.Core or loaded from a JSON file.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
This guide is for people who build and run workflows.

  • Getting started: start the app, open a sample, build a first workflow.
  • The editor: palette, canvas, side panel, running and testing, groups.
  • Items and expressions: the data model, {{ }} expressions and the Code node.
  • Triggers and webhooks: start workflows from outside and answer the caller.
  • Credentials: store logins and use them in nodes.
  • Error handling: retries, error outputs and error workflows.
  • Executions: what is running, the history and sensitive data.
  • Recipes: the sample workflows, to download.
  • Node reference: every node with its parameters (generated, English only).

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
A credential holds the login data a node needs: a password, a token, an SMTP server, a connection string. You create it once and select it in nodes. The secret never appears in the workflow itself.

Open Credentials in the top bar to see them.

docs.title: Create a credential
docs.text:
1. Click New credential.
  2. Choose the type and give it a name.
  3. Fill in the fields. Secret fields (passwords, tokens) are masked.
  4. Save.

The list shows the name, the type and the id of each credential. The id is what the workflow stores and what an administrator enters in the configuration (for example for a Git server).

Important

After saving, secret fields are never shown again. To change a secret, enter it anew. Credentials are stored encrypted on the server.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Type Used by Fields Basic Auth HTTP Request, Webhook Trigger, Git servers user name, password Bearer Token HTTP Request, Webhook Trigger, Git servers token API Key Header HTTP Request, Webhook Trigger header name, value Connection String SQL provider (sqlserver, postgres or sqlite), connection string SMTP Send Email host, port, security (auto, SSL on connect, StartTLS, none), user name, password, sender address

The exact fields are listed in the credential types of the node reference.

docs.title: Use a credential
docs.text:
Parameters that need a credential show a drop-down with the credentials of the right types. Select one. The node's hints tell you when it is missing.

  • HTTP Request: the credential authenticates the call (Basic, Bearer or an API key header).
  • Webhook Trigger: callers must send the matching Authorization header (or API key header). Without a credential the webhook is public.
  • SQL: the connection string and provider.
  • Send Email: the SMTP server and login.
  • Script nodes: the credential's fields are passed to the script as PIPE_CREDENTIAL_<FIELD> environment variables. Values are masked in the output and in the logs.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• A credential belongs to the whole app, not to a workflow. Whoever can edit workflows can use every credential, but not read its secrets.
  • Workflow files contain only the credential id. You can share them without sharing secrets; the other installation has to create a credential with the same id or select another one.
  • If you move an installation, copy the credentials and the keys folder together (see the Admin Guide).

docs.title: Files and data
docs.text: Files travel through a workflow as attachments of items (see Items and expressions). A webhook upload, a mail attachment, an HTTP response or Read File gives you one; Send Email, Write File and HTTP Request take one. The nodes on this page turn attachments into items and back, and work with dates, hashes and archives. The sample Data Tools uses all of them (Recipes).

docs.title: Extract from File
docs.text:
Reads the attachment data (setting Binary property) of each item in a format and makes items of it.

Format Becomes Settings CSV one item per row; values are text Header row, Delimiter (empty: detected from the first row), Encoding Excel one item per row; numbers stay numbers, dates become ISO text Header row, Sheet (empty: the first). Needs the Office plugin. JSON an object is one item, an array one item per element Encoding XML the whole document as one item, or one item per Item element Item element, Always array, Encoding Text one item with the content in text Encoding

Output Field keeps the input item and puts all rows into one field (rows) instead. Use it when the item carries more than the file, for example the sender of a mail.

Text is read as UTF-8 unless the file starts with a byte order mark or Encoding says otherwise, for example windows-1252 for CSV files saved by an older Excel.

docs.title: XML as items
docs.text:
XML elements become JSON like this:

<order id="7" xmlns:x="urn:x"><line>Pen</line><line>Ink</line><x:note>fast</x:note></order>

{ "@id": "7", "@xmlns:x": "urn:x", "line": ["Pen", "Ink"], "x:note": "fast" }

Attributes start with @, text next to attributes or elements is in #text, repeated elements become arrays. An element that occurs once is a single value: list it in Always array (e.g. line) when your expressions expect an array.

docs.title: Convert to File
docs.text:
Writes items into an attachment (data, file name in File name, with expressions).
