  • CSV and Excel always make one file of all items. The columns are all fields of the items in the order they appear; nested objects are written as JSON. Excel can put the items on one sheet per value of a field (Sheet per field, e.g. region).
  • JSON writes an array of all items, or with Files = Each item each item as an object.
  • XML writes all items as Item element below Root element (<items><item>…</item></items>), or one document per item. An item read by Extract from File ({ "order": { … } }) is written back with the same root.
  • Text writes the field Text field (text) of the items, one per line.

docs.title: Date & Time
docs.text:
Works on a date and writes the result into Target field.

Operation Result Now the current time, in Time zone if set Format the date as text in Pattern (e.g. dd.MM.yyyy HH:mm), in Culture (e.g. de-DE for German month names) and Time zone Parse text in Pattern as ISO date; text without an offset is in Time zone Add, Subtract Amount of Unit; months and years only in whole numbers Difference from Date to Until (empty: now) in Unit; months and years are counted as whole calendar units Convert time zone the same moment in Time zone Start of the start of the day, week (Monday), month, … in Time zone

Dates are read as ISO 8601 (2026-11-02T08:30:00+01:00), common text forms, or Unix seconds or milliseconds. Results are ISO 8601 with offset, so the next node reads them without a pattern. Time zones are IANA ids like Europe/Vienna or Windows ids. Patterns follow .NET: yyyy year, MM month, dd day, HH hour, mm minute, dddd weekday name, MMMM month name.

docs.title: Crypto
docs.text:
Operation Result Hash SHA-256, SHA-512, SHA-1 or MD5 of Value or of an attachment, as hex or Base64 HMAC a signature of Value or an attachment with Secret, e.g. to check a webhook signature UUID a new random id Base64 encode / decode Value or an attachment as Base64, or Base64 back to text

Take the HMAC secret from a secret variable ({{ $vars.WEBHOOK_SECRET }}, see Variables and environments), so it isn't stored in the workflow. MD5 and SHA-1 are fine for checksums, not for security.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text:
Operation Result Zip the attachments of each item, or of all items (Zip = All items), in one ZIP archive (Archive name) Unzip one item per file of the archive, with the file in data and fileName, path, size; or all files as attachments of the input item GZip / GUnzip compresses or decompresses one attachment

Unpacking stops with an error when the content gets larger than Max size (500 MB), so a small archive can't fill the server. Archives are never unpacked to disk: paths in the archive are only text in the items.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text: You build a workflow in the editor: nodes on a canvas, connected by lines. Open it from the workflow list, or create a new workflow there.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Area Purpose Palette (left) All node types by category, with a search field. Hover a node for its description. Canvas (middle) The workflow. Nodes show their name and type; ports are the dots on their edges. Side panel (right) With no node selected: the settings of the workflow. With a node selected: its parameters, settings and run result. Toolbar (top) Back, undo and redo, paste, add a note, show or hide the palette and the side panel, the Active switch, Save and Run.

The palette and the side panel can be resized by dragging the thin bar next to them. A double click resets the width. Two toolbar buttons hide and show them, to give the canvas more room; the browser keeps that choice. A large workflow is shown at 70 % at least, so the names stay readable; scroll the canvas to see the rest.

The icon at the right of the top bar switches the colors: following the system, light or dark. The browser keeps your choice.

docs.title: Building a workflow
docs.text:
1. Add a node: click it in the palette. It appears on the canvas; drag it where you want it.
  2. Connect nodes: drag from an output port (right edge) to an input port (left edge) of another node. Items flow along the line. A node with several outputs (If, Switch) has one port per output.
  3. Edit a node: click it. The side panel shows its Parameters, Settings and Run tabs.
  4. Delete: select a node or a line and press Delete, or use the trash icon in the side panel.
  5. Save: the Save button or Ctrl+S stores the workflow. If you leave the editor or close the tab with unsaved changes, it asks first. Triggers of an active workflow (Cron, Webhook) are armed when you save.

Tip

Hold Shift while you drag a node onto an existing line to insert it there. The line lights up before you drop.

The first node of a workflow is a trigger (see Triggers and webhooks). A workflow can have several triggers; a manual run starts at every node that has no incoming connection.

docs.title: Copy, paste and undo
docs.text:
• Copy a selection with Ctrl+C on the canvas, paste with Ctrl+V. Pasting also works into another workflow, so you can move parts between workflows. The toolbar has a paste button too.
  • Duplicate a node with the icon in the side panel.
  • Undo and redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z on the canvas, or the toolbar) work for every change to the workflow. Typing into the fields of one node counts as one step.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Use the note button in the toolbar to put a sticky note on the canvas, for example to explain why a filter is there or what to set up first. Select a note to change its text, color (yellow, green, blue, red, purple, gray) and size in the side panel; drag it like a node. Notes lie behind the nodes, have no ports and don't affect a run. They can be copied, pasted, duplicated, deleted and undone like nodes. Without the editor role you see them read only.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
The form is generated from the node. Most text fields accept expressions: {{ $json.total * 1.2 }} is evaluated for each item (see Items and expressions). In the Run tab you can click a field of the input to insert it as an expression into the parameter you edited last.

Changes take effect while you type; you don't have to leave a field before you select another node or save.

Expressions are tinted in their field. After a run, a line below the field shows its value for the first input item of the node, for example = Hello Hello Pipe!. $node["Name"] can't be resolved there and shows a warning; the run itself is not affected.

Code fields (the JavaScript of the Code node, the SQL of the SQL node, raw JSON) open in a code editor with syntax highlighting, line numbers and the usual editor keys (Tab to indent, Ctrl+F to find, Alt+Up/Down to move lines). The field grows with its content; the icon above it opens a large editor, and Apply takes its text over.

Some nodes show hints above their parameters, for example the URL of a webhook or a warning that it has no credential.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Meaning Name Unique in the workflow. Expressions use it: $node["Name"]. Notes Free text for yourself. Disabled The node passes its items through without running. Always execute Run the node even when it received no items. On error, Retries, Timeout See Error handling.

docs.title: Run
docs.text: After a run, this tab shows the Input the node received, the Output it produced per port and its Logs. Items can be shown as JSON or as text. A node that wrote output while it was running (for example a script) shows it live.

docs.title: Running and testing
docs.text:
• Run starts the workflow from the editor, in the environment chosen next to the button (see Variables and environments). Nodes show their state: green for success, red for an error, gray when they got no items and were skipped. A badge on each output shows how many items it produced.
  • Run to here (play icon in the side panel) runs only the selected node and the nodes it depends on.
  • Pin output (in the Run tab) keeps a node's output. Manual runs then use the pinned items instead of running the node again, which is useful for nodes that call a slow or costly API. Pinned nodes show a pin. Runs started by a trigger ignore pinned data, so production runs never use test data.
  • Closing the green or red result chip above the canvas clears the display of the last run.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Workflows are sorted into groups, shown as tiles on the start page. A workflow is in at most one group. Change it with the Group field of the workflow panel, Move to group in the list, or by dragging a row onto a tile.

Open a group to see its workflows and to create new ones in it. Deleting a group never deletes its workflows. The group dialog (pencil on the tile) sets name, color, the portal roles and what its workflows inherit: the environment, variables and the error workflow.

docs.title: Workflow settings
docs.text:
Select no node (click the empty canvas) to see the settings of the workflow:

Setting Meaning Name, Description Shown in the list. Max concurrent runs How many runs of this workflow may be active at the same time (default 1). More wait in the queue or are skipped; a webhook caller gets 429 then. Max queued runs How many triggered runs (cron, webhook, error workflow) may wait for a free slot, in the order they arrived (default 0: skip them). Waiting runs show as Queued under "Running now" and can be stopped there. Manual runs are never queued. Save item data of executions Switch off to store only statuses, counts and logs in the history (sensitive data). Group The group on the start page. Environment The environment of triggered runs, or Inherit from the group or the instance. See Variables and environments. Webhook callers may choose Environments a webhook caller can pick with X-Pipe-Environment. Variables Variables of this workflow, one value per environment. Error workflow Started when a triggered run fails, see Error handling. Inherit (the default) takes the group's or the instance's, None switches it off. Publish in portal Makes the workflow visible to users in the user portal, in the category of its group. Then you choose who may see it (Only these roles), whether users wait or the run goes to the background, the wait timeout, whether users may switch, whether they may stop the run and whether only one run may go at a time. The form comes from a Form Trigger node, the result from a Result node. Without a Form Trigger the workflow starts without input. See REST API. Executions The history of this workflow, see Executions.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text: A node can fail: a script exits with a non-zero code, an HTTP call returns an error, a database is down. What happens next is decided per node, and per workflow by an optional error workflow.

docs.title: Node settings
docs.text:
Open a node and switch to the Settings tab.

Setting Meaning Retries, Retry delay (ms) The node is run again after a failure, up to this many times. Backoff, Max delay (ms) Fixed delay waits the same time before every retry. Exponential doubles it after every failed attempt (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, …), up to the max delay (0 = no limit). Shown when Retries is above 0. Timeout (seconds) The node is canceled after this time. 0 means no timeout. On error What the workflow does when the node still fails (see below).

docs.title: On error
docs.text:
Mode What happens Run status Stop the execution (default) The run is canceled. Nodes after the failed one never run. Error Continue with the input items The error is recorded on the node, and the node passes its input items on its normal output (a script node passes its results, for example the exit code). The workflow goes on. Success Route items to an error output The node gets a second output port, error. The items go there instead of the normal output, each with an error field { "message": …, "type": … }. The normal output stays empty. Success

A node whose inputs are all empty is skipped, and so are the nodes after it. That is what makes the error output useful: connect one branch to the normal output and another to the error output. Only the branch that receives items runs.

Note

With Continue or Error output, the run counts as successful. That has two consequences: the error workflow is not started, and a webhook caller does not get a 500 unless you send one yourself.

docs.title: Error workflows
docs.text:
An error workflow is a normal workflow that starts with an Error Trigger. Choose it in the workflow panel of the failing workflow (Error workflow), for all workflows of a group in the group dialog, or for the whole instance in the configuration (Pipe:ErrorWorkflowId). A workflow uses the first one set on workflow → group → instance; None on the workflow switches it off.

  • It runs when a run of the workflow fails and was started by a trigger (cron, webhook) or is a replay. Runs you start by hand in the editor don't start it.
  • A failing sub-workflow doesn't start it: its caller fails too and reports it, with the sub-workflow in subWorkflow. If the caller catches the failure (Continue or Error output on Execute Workflow), nothing is reported.

  • It receives one item that describes the failed run, for example to send a mail with the name of the workflow and the failed node:

    { "workflow": { "id": "…", "name": "…" },
  "execution": { "id": "…", "mode": "…", "environment": "…", "startedAt": "…", "error": "…", "url": "…" },
  "node": { "id": "…", "name": "…", "error": "…" },
  "subWorkflow": { "id": "…", "name": "…", "executionId": "…", "error": "…", "node": { … } },
  "suppressed": 0 }

    Use it in expressions, for example {{ $json.workflow.name }} and {{ $json.execution.error }}. url links to the failed run when Pipe:PublicUrl is configured; subWorkflow is only there when a sub-workflow failed. - Throttle minutes on the Error Trigger (default 15) starts it at most once in that time per failed workflow. Failures in between are counted in suppressed of the next run. Set 0 to report every failure. - Add a Recovery Trigger to the same workflow to be told when the failed workflow runs successfully again; see Failure notifications. - A failure of the error workflow itself is only written to the application log. A workflow is never its own error workflow. - It does not change the result of the failed run. The run stays Error.

The samples Error Mail, Error Teams and Error Slack send notifications, Error Alerts writes to the log; see Failure notifications.

docs.title: Answering a webhook after a failure
docs.text:
A webhook that waits for a Respond to Webhook node (Triggers and webhooks) gets 500 when the run fails, because the Respond node is never reached. The error workflow doesn't help here: it runs separately and can't answer the call.

To control the answer, handle the error inside the workflow:

  1. Set On error of the node that can fail to Route items to an error output.
  2. Connect the normal output to a Respond to Webhook node with status 200.
  3. Connect the error output to a second Respond to Webhook node. Choose the status and the body yourself, for example status 502 with Custom body {{ { error: $json.error.message } }}.
  4. Optional: put a Send Email node (or a Log node) on the error branch before the Respond node, to be notified.

Because the branch that gets no items is skipped, exactly one of the two Respond nodes runs.

Tip

With Continue with the input items you can keep one Respond node. Test the result in the node after the one that can fail (for example with an If node that checks the exit code) and switch the status code with an expression.

If you want both a clean answer and the error workflow, send the notification from the error branch, as in step 4. The error workflow only starts for runs that end with Error.

docs.title: Finding out what failed
docs.text:
• In the editor, a failed node is shown with a red frame and an error badge. Its Run tab shows the input, the output and the log, including the error message.
  • Webhook answers with 500 contain the executionId. Open that execution in the history.
  • Scripts: a non-zero exit code or an output line matching the error pattern fails the node. The output of the script is in the node's log.

docs.title: Executions
docs.text: An execution is one run of a workflow, started by the editor, a trigger or another workflow. gView.Pipe records every execution with what each node received, produced and logged.

docs.title: Running now
docs.text:
The start page lists every run in progress, whatever started it (the editor, Cron, a webhook or a sub-workflow). Each entry shows the workflow, its current node and the latest output line. The top bar shows n running.

Click a run to watch it in the editor, live. In the editor you can also stop it. Runs started by a webhook continue even when the caller disconnects, so stopping is the way to end one early.

Note

The list shows runs of this app instance. A finished run stays visible for a minute.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
The workflow panel of the editor (select no node) lists the executions of the workflow, newest first, with status, start time, environment, how it was started (Manual, Trigger for Cron and Webhook, Sub-workflow, Error workflow, Replay, API with the name of the API key) and the duration. The field above the list filters by environment. The last 50 are kept, unless the workflow panel (Executions kept, Days kept) or the configuration says otherwise.

Click an execution to open it on the canvas: every node shows its state and counts, and you can open each node's Run tab to see the input, output and logs of that run. A note appears when the workflow was changed since the run, because some nodes may no longer exist.

Status Meaning Success The run finished. Individual nodes may have failed if they use Continue or Error output. Error A node failed with Stop the execution. The failed node is marked red. Canceled Someone stopped the run. Running Still in progress.

Click the x next to the result chip above the canvas to clear the display and go back to the plain workflow.

docs.title: All executions
docs.text: Executions in the navigation lists the executions of all workflows, newest first: workflow, status, how it was started, environment, start, duration and the failed node. Filter by workflow or group, status, how it was started and time range (the last 7 days at first); Load more fetches older ones. Click a row to open the execution in the editor.

docs.title: Replay
docs.text:
A replay runs a stored execution again, for example after you fixed the cause of a failure:

  • It runs the saved, current workflow, not the version of the original run.
  • It uses the stored data of the original run and runs in its environment.
  • It behaves like a triggered run: pinned data is ignored, and the error workflow starts when it fails.
  • It is listed as started by Replay and marked with the replay icon.

Where you start it:

Where What runs again Replay button of a row, or several selected rows on the Executions page The whole workflow, with the trigger output of the original run. Several replays run one after the other, oldest first. Replay from failed node on the Executions page Failed executions from their failed node, the others from the start. Replay icon next to the result chip in the editor The whole workflow; the red icon next to it replays from the failed node. Replay from here in the toolbar of a selected node, while a run is shown This node and everything after it. All other nodes take their outputs from the shown run.

A replay waits until the workflow has a free run slot (Max concurrent runs) instead of being skipped. In the editor, save your changes first: the replay runs the saved workflow.

Warning

Executions stored without item data (Save item data of executions switched off) can't be replayed. Files of a run (binary data) are not kept after it ends: a node that reads such a file in a replay fails.

docs.title: Sensitive data
docs.text: Items of an execution are stored in the history, so they stay readable for everyone who can use the editor. Switch off Save item data of executions in the workflow panel if items contain sensitive data: then only statuses, counts and logs are stored. Secrets from webhook headers (Authorization, Cookie) never reach the items.

docs.title: Executions and restarts
docs.text: Running executions live in the memory of the app. When the app restarts, they end. A Wait node that is waiting loses its run. Finished executions are kept in files and survive a restart.

docs.title: Items
docs.text:
Data flows through a workflow as items. An item is a JSON object, plus optional binary attachments (files). A connection carries a list of items, and a node receives all items of its inputs at once.

{ "id": 1, "customer": "Ada", "total": 120, "country": "AT" }

Most nodes process each item on its own: the Set node adds fields to every item, If sends each item to true or false. A few nodes work on the whole list: Aggregate collects many items into one, Split Out turns one item into many, Limit and Sort change the list.

Items are copied on their way into a node, so parallel branches can't change each other's data.

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
Any text parameter can contain expressions in double curly braces. The content is JavaScript:

Hello {{ $json.customer }}, your total is {{ $json.total * 1.2 }} EUR
  • A parameter that consists of one expression keeps the type of the result: {{ $json.total * 1.2 }} is a number, {{ $json.tags }} an array.
  • With text around the expressions, the result is text.
  • Expressions run once per item, with that item as $json.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Variable Meaning $json The JSON of the current item. $itemIndex The position of the current item in the list (from 0). $input.first(), $input.all() The first item or all items of the node's input. $node["Name"].json The first item that the node Name produced. .all is the list of all its items. $workflow Id and name of the workflow. $execution Id of the current run. $now The current time as ISO text. $vars.NAME A variable of the workflow, its group or the instance, see Variables and environments. $environment The environment of the run, for example PROD.

There is no $env: the environment variables of the server often contain secrets. Use variables for shared values and credentials for secrets.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Goal Expression A nested field {{ $json.address.city }} Safe access when the field may be missing {{ $json.address?.city ?? 'unknown' }} Calculate {{ Math.round($json.total * 1.2 * 100) / 100 }} Join text {{ $json.first + ' ' + $json.last }} Condition {{ $json.total > 100 ? 'big' : 'small' }} Data of an earlier node {{ $node["Products"].json.name }} Webhook body {{ $json.body?.name ?? 'stranger' }} Count the items {{ $input.all().length }}

Warning

Accessing a field of something that doesn't exist is an error, as in JavaScript: $json.missing.deeper fails if missing isn't there. Use ?.: $json.missing?.deeper.

Values are copied into the expression: changing $json inside an expression doesn't change the item. Expressions can't use the network or files and are stopped after one second.

docs.title: The editor helps
docs.text:
Autocomplete: inside {{ }} the field suggests what you can write: the fields of the node's input ($json.…), the output of earlier nodes ($node["Name"].json.…), the variables of the environment ($vars.…, secret ones without their value) and the global names ($now, $workflow, …). Each suggestion shows its type and a sample value from the last run.

  • The list opens after {{, . and [", or with Ctrl+Space.
  • ↑ ↓ choose, Enter or Tab inserts, Esc closes.
  • Typing {{ adds the closing }}.
  • The fields come from the run shown in the editor, or from pinned data. Without one, run the workflow once or use Run to here on the node before.
  • Code fields (the Code node) offer the same, plus items[0].… in All items mode.

Below the field, = … shows the value of the expression for the first input item of the last run.

In the Run tab of a node, click a field of the input to put the matching expression into the parameter you edited last.

docs.title: The Code node
docs.text:
For anything larger than an expression, the Code node runs JavaScript. It has two modes:

  • All items: your code gets items (an array with the JSON of all input items) and returns an array of objects, which become the output items.
  • Each item: your code runs once per item with $json and returns an object, or null to drop the item.
// mode: all items
const orders = items.filter(order => order.total > 100);
console.log(`${orders.length} big orders`);
return orders.map(order => ({ ...order, big: true }));

// mode: each item
if ($json.country === 'DE') return null;
return { ...$json, vat: $json.total * 0.2 };
  • console.log writes to the Logs of the node.
  • The variables of expressions ($node, $workflow, $now, …) are available.
  • The code is not scanned for {{ }}; write plain JavaScript.
  • A Code node may run up to 30 seconds. It can't use the network or files: use the HTTP Request or Read File nodes for that.
  • Attachments of an item are kept when the number of items stays the same.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text: Files (for example from a webhook upload or the Read File node) travel with the item as binary attachments by name. They are not part of the JSON. Nodes such as Write File and Send Email can use them. The bytes of attachments exist only while the execution runs; in the history you see that an attachment existed, but can't download it afterwards.

docs.title: Start the app
docs.text:
dotnet run --project src/gView.Pipe.Shell

Open the URL printed in the console. With the http profile that is http://localhost:5240; with the https profile https://localhost:7240. Your administrator gives you the address of an installed instance (see the Admin Guide).

docs.title: The sample workflows
docs.text:
On the first start with an empty store, gView.Pipe copies a set of sample workflows into the group Samples:

Workflow What it shows Hello Pipe A manual trigger, Set and Log. The best first workflow to open. Code Transform JavaScript, Switch and Merge. Item Tools Split Out, Remove Duplicates, Sort, Limit and Aggregate. Sub-workflow Demo, Price Calculator A workflow that calls another one per batch of items. Failures go to Error Alerts, an error workflow. API Demo A webhook that answers with Respond to Webhook nodes. Webhook Demo A webhook that answers with a greeting. It is inactive until you switch it on. File Export Writes orders as CSV and reads them back. Error Mail, Error Teams, Error Slack Error workflows that send a failure notification. Their sending node is disabled until you set them up.

docs.title: Build your first workflow
docs.text:
1. On the start page, create a workflow and open it in the editor.
  2. Add a trigger node from the palette. Manual Trigger is the simplest: the workflow starts when you run it.
  3. Add more nodes and connect an output port of one node to an input port of the next. Items flow along the connections.
  4. Click a node to edit its parameters in the side panel. In any text field, {{ … }} is a JavaScript expression that is evaluated against the current item, for example {{ $json.total * 1.2 }}.
  5. Run the workflow. Each node shows the items it received, the items it produced and the log lines it wrote.

Click a node and open its Run tab to see what it received (Input), what it produced (Output) and what it logged (Logs):

docs.title: Triggers need an active workflow
docs.text: A manual run works at any time. Cron and Webhook triggers only fire while the workflow is Active: switch it on with the Active switch in the editor. See Triggers and webhooks.

docs.title: What next
docs.text:
• Triggers and webhooks: start workflows from outside and answer the caller.
  • Error handling: retries, error outputs and error workflows.

docs.title: Failure notifications
docs.text:
When a scheduled or webhook-triggered workflow fails, nobody is watching the editor. An error workflow can send a message instead: a mail, a Teams post or a Slack message. The samples group contains one for each.

Sample Sends Needs Error Mail a mail with workflow, environment, node, error and a link an SMTP credential and the variable ALERT_MAIL_TO Error Teams an Adaptive Card to a Teams channel the secret variable ALERT_TEAMS_URL Error Slack a message to a Slack channel the secret variable ALERT_SLACK_URL Error Alerts a line in the application log nothing

docs.title: Setting up
docs.text:
1. Open the sample, for example Error Mail. Its sending node is disabled so that a fresh installation sends nothing.
  2. Set what it needs:
    • Error Mail: choose the SMTP credential in the node Send Mail, and define the variable ALERT_MAIL_TO (one or more addresses, separated by commas) on the Variables page. Different values per environment are possible, for example a team mailbox for PROD.
    • Error Teams: in Teams, add the workflow Post to a channel when a webhook request is received to the channel and copy its URL. Define it as the secret variable ALERT_TEAMS_URL.
    • Error Slack: create an incoming webhook in your Slack app and define its URL as the secret variable ALERT_SLACK_URL.
  3. Enable the sending node (select it, Settings, switch off Disabled) and save.

  4. Choose the error workflow where it should apply:

    • for one workflow: Error workflow in its workflow panel;
    • for a group: Error workflow in the group dialog (pencil on the group tile);
    • for all workflows: Pipe:ErrorWorkflowId in pipe.config, for example "error-mail" (Configuration).

    A workflow uses the first one set on workflow → group → instance. None on a workflow switches notifications off for it, for example for a test workflow. 5. Ask the administrator to set Pipe:PublicUrl to the address users open the app at. Then the messages contain a link to the failed run.

Copy a sample rather than editing it when you need several variants, for example different recipients per group.

docs.title: How often messages are sent
docs.text:
The Throttle minutes of the Error Trigger (default 15) limit the messages per failed workflow: after a message, further failures of the same workflow are only counted for that time. The next message says how many there were (suppressed). A workflow that fails every minute therefore sends one message per quarter of an hour, not 15. Set 0 to get every failure.

Other things that keep the noise down:

  • Runs you start in the editor never send messages.
  • A failing sub-workflow is reported once, by the workflow that called it; the message names the sub-workflow and its failed node.
  • A node with Continue or Error output doesn't fail the run, so it isn't reported. Send a message from its error branch if you need one (Error handling).

docs.title: Back to normal
docs.text:
An alarm should also end. Put a Recovery Trigger into the same workflow as the Error Trigger and connect it to a message, like the second branch of the three samples (disabled until you set them up). It starts when a workflow that failed runs successfully again.

  • It only reports a recovery when a failure was reported before: if the throttle swallowed all failures, or no error workflow applied, nobody hears about the recovery either.
  • Only runs by trigger, replay or the API count. A run you start in the editor neither starts nor ends a failure.
  • The state is kept on disk (data/health), so it survives a restart.
  • The item is { workflow, execution, failedSince, failedExecution, failures }; execution.url and failedExecution.url link to the runs with Pipe:PublicUrl.
Expression Value {{ $json.failedSince }} start of the first failed run {{ $json.failures }} failed runs since then, reported or not

docs.title: Trying it out
docs.text: Start the developer containers with Mailpit (ADD_MAILPIT in the AppHost, see the Developer Guide) and create an SMTP credential for localhost, port 1025, without TLS. Set up Error Mail with it, make a workflow with a Cron or Webhook Trigger fail (for example a Code node with throw new Error('test')), and let it run by its trigger or replay a failed run. The mail appears at http://localhost:8025.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text:
Any workflow that starts with an Error Trigger is an error workflow. Its item is described in Error handling. Useful expressions:

Expression Value {{ $json.workflow.name }} name of the failed workflow {{ $json.execution.environment }} environment of the run, for example PROD {{ $json.node?.name ?? '-' }} the failed node, if known {{ $json.execution.error }} the error message {{ $json.execution.url ?? '' }} link to the run (with Pipe:PublicUrl) {{ $json.suppressed }} failures not reported since the last message

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
The sample workflows that come with gView.Pipe double as recipes. Each one solves a small task and teaches a few nodes. They are in the group Samples of an empty installation, and you can download the JSON files here.

Using a downloaded file

There is no import button yet. Copy the file into the workflows folder inside the data folder of the app (see the Admin Guide) and reload the workflow list; restart the app if the workflow does not appear. The file name is the id of the workflow. Workflows that call other workflows (Execute Workflow, error workflows) refer to them by id, so keep the ids.

docs.title: Hello Pipe
docs.text:
Manual trigger → Set → If → Log. Download

The first workflow to open. Set Greeting adds fields to the item (greeting uses an expression), If ({{ $json.score }} greater than 10) sends the item to true or false, and one of two Log nodes writes the result. Run it and look at the Run tab of each node. The branch that gets no items is skipped (gray).

docs.title: Code Transform
docs.text:
Code → Switch → Set → Merge → Log. Download

A Code node generates four orders. Switch routes them by {{ $json.country }}: orders from AT go to one Set node (20 % VAT), orders from DE to another (19 %), and Merge joins the two branches again. Orders from other countries leave through the fallback output, which is not connected here, so they are dropped. A good model for "different handling per kind of item".

docs.title: Item Tools
docs.text:
Split Out → Remove Duplicates → Sort → Limit → Aggregate. Download

Orders contain a list of order lines. Split Out turns each line into its own item, Remove Duplicates keeps one item per sku, Sort orders by price (descending), Limit keeps the first three, and Aggregate collects the SKUs into one item.

docs.title: Sub-workflow Demo and Price Calculator
docs.text:
Execute Workflow per batch. Sub-workflow Demo · Price Calculator · Error Alerts

Price Calculator starts with an Execute Workflow Trigger and adds VAT. Sub-workflow Demo calls it with Execute Workflow in mode batches (two items per call). That is how you build a loop: call a sub-workflow per item or per batch. The demo names Error Alerts as its error workflow: if the run fails, Error Alerts writes the failure to the log.

docs.title: API Demo
docs.text:
Webhook → If → Respond to Webhook. Download

A small API: POST /webhook/api/greet with { "name": "Ada" } answers 200 with a greeting, and without a name 400 with an error text. The trigger waits for a Respond to Webhook node (Using respond node). Activate the workflow first.

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5240/webhook/api/greet -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Ada"}'

See Triggers and webhooks.

docs.title: Webhook Demo
docs.text:
Webhook → Set. Download

The shortest webhook: POST /webhook/demo answers with a greeting. The trigger is set to When finished, so the caller receives the items of the last node. The workflow is inactive until you switch it on.

docs.title: File Export
docs.text:
Code → Write File → Read File. Download

Writes orders as a CSV file into the released folder files (exports/orders-<date>.csv) and reads the file back as items. The folder name files has to be released by the administrator (Pipe:FileRoots), see the Admin Guide.

docs.title: Data Tools
docs.text:
Code → Date & Time → Date & Time → Crypto → Convert to File → Compression (zip) → Compression (unzip) → Extract from File. Download

Builds two orders, adds a due date 14 days later and formats it for Vienna, adds a SHA-256 checksum, writes the orders as a CSV attachment, zips and unzips it and reads the CSV back. No folder is involved: the files exist only as attachments of the run. See Files and data.

docs.title: Build your own
docs.text:
• Call an API on a schedule: Cron Trigger → HTTP Request → Code or Set → Send Email.
  • React to a webhook and answer: Webhook Trigger (Using respond node) → your nodes → Respond to Webhook, with an error output for failures (Error handling).
  • Run a script nightly and get a mail on failure: Cron Trigger → Run Script, with an error workflow that sends the mail.
  • Accept a CSV upload and mail it back as Excel: Webhook Trigger → Extract from File (CSV) → your nodes → Convert to File (Excel) → Send Email with the attachment data.
  • Copy rows between databases: Cron Trigger → SQL (select) → SQL (insert, once per item).

docs.title: Triggers and webhooks
docs.text:
A trigger is the first node of a workflow. It decides when the workflow starts.

Trigger Starts the workflow Manual Trigger When you run it in the editor. Cron Trigger On a schedule (5 or 6 field cron expression), while the workflow is active. Webhook Trigger When its URL is called, while the workflow is active. Execute Workflow Trigger When another workflow calls this one with the Execute Workflow node. Error Trigger When a run of another workflow fails (see Error handling).

docs.title: Webhook Trigger
docs.text:
A Webhook Trigger makes the workflow callable at

<server address>/webhook/<path>

The editor shows the exact URL as a hint next to the parameters.

Parameter Meaning Path Letters, digits, _, - and /, lower case. Must be unique across all active workflows. A random path is suggested for a new node. HTTP method POST by default, or GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, or any method. Respond When and how the caller gets an answer (see below). Wait timeout (seconds) How long the caller waits in the modes that wait. After that the caller gets 202 and the run goes on. Credential Basic Auth, Bearer Token or API Key Header. Without one, anyone who knows the URL can start the workflow.

Warning

A webhook without a credential is public. The editor warns you about it.

docs.title: The request as an item
docs.text:
The trigger turns the call into one item:

{
  "method": "POST",
  "path": "orders/new",
  "query": { "id": "7" },
  "headers": { "content-type": "application/json" },
  "body": { "customer": "ACME" },
  "receivedAt": "2026-11-01T10:15:00.0000000+00:00"
}
  • A JSON body (Content-Type contains json) becomes an object in body. Form fields become an object. Any other body is text.
  • Uploaded files become binary attachments of the item.
  • The headers authorization, proxy-authorization, cookie and the API key header are removed, so secrets never end up in the execution history.
  • Bodies larger than 10 MB are rejected with 413.

docs.title: Answering the caller
docs.text:
The Respond parameter decides what the caller receives.

Mode The caller gets Immediately 202 with { "executionId": …, "status": "started" } straight away. The workflow runs in the background. Whether it succeeds is not reported to the caller. When finished The items of the node that finished last: one item as an object, several as an array. If the run fails, the caller gets 500. Using respond node The answer of a Respond to Webhook node in the workflow.

In both waiting modes the caller gets 202 with "status": "running" when the run takes longer than the timeout. The run is never canceled when the caller disconnects.

When the workflow is busy and has a queue (Max queued runs in the workflow panel), the run waits for a free slot. Immediately then answers "status": "queued". In the waiting modes the time in the queue counts against the timeout: if the run still waits when it passes, the caller gets 503 with Retry-After and the run leaves the queue.

docs.title: Respond to Webhook
docs.text:
The Respond to Webhook node sends the answer in the mode Using respond node. It lets you choose the status code, headers and body:

Parameter Meaning Respond with The first item, all items as an array, a custom body or no body. Body For custom body: JSON or an expression, evaluated against the first item. Status code 100 to 599. Supports expressions. Headers Optional response headers. A text body with a non-JSON Content-Type (for example text/html) is sent as is.

The items pass through the node, so the workflow can continue after it has answered.

Important

The answer only exists if a Respond to Webhook node runs. When a node before it fails with the error mode Stop the execution, the run ends there, the Respond node never runs, and the caller gets 500 with the error message. To answer in a failure case too, see Answering a webhook after a failure.

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text:
Code Reason 200 Answer of the workflow (When finished) or of a Respond to Webhook node. 202 Started or queued (Immediately), or the timeout passed while the run goes on. 400 The header X-Pipe-Environment names an environment the workflow doesn't allow. 401 The credential is missing or wrong. 404 No active webhook at this path. 405 The method does not match the trigger. 413 The body is too large. 429 The workflow is already running, its limit of concurrent runs is reached (default 1) and its queue is full or off. 503 The run still waited in the queue when the timeout passed; it was taken out of the queue. Try again after Retry-After seconds. 500 The run failed, or ended without reaching a Respond to Webhook node. The body contains the error and the execution id.

The 500 body looks like { "error": "…", "executionId": "…" }. Look the execution id up in the execution history to see which node failed.

docs.title: Choosing the environment
docs.text:
A webhook run uses the effective environment of the workflow (see Variables and environments). To let callers choose another one, for example to test a system against the test database, list it under Webhook callers may choose in the workflow panel. The caller then sends the header:

X-Pipe-Environment: TEST

An environment that isn't listed is rejected with 400, never silently replaced. The header is checked after the credential, so a caller without access learns nothing about the environments.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5240/webhook/demo -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Ada"}'

In Windows PowerShell, Invoke-RestMethod hides the body of an error answer. Use curl.exe -i (with -k for the development certificate on https://localhost:7240) to see the status code and the body.

docs.title: Variables and environments
docs.text: Many workflows need the same values: a database server, a share, the URL of an API. Variables hold them in one place, and environments (for example TEST and PROD) choose which value applies. A workflow can then run against the test database without changing any node.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
The administrator lists the environments in the configuration. DEFAULT always exists. The instance runs in exactly one of them; that is set by the administrator and can't be changed in the app.

Groups and workflows set an environment or inherit it (the default):

  1. the environment of the workflow, if it sets one,
  2. otherwise the environment of its group, if that sets one,
  3. otherwise the environment of the instance.

The result is the effective environment. The workflow list shows it as a colored badge (PROD red, STAGE orange, TEST blue, DEFAULT gray). A badge that is only outlined is inherited; its tooltip names where from. Group tiles show the environment of the group the same way.

Moving a workflow into another group can change an inherited environment. The app then asks before it moves the workflow ("runs in PROD instead of TEST").

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Variables are defined on three levels, each with one value per environment:

Level Where Instance Variables in the menu bar, and the configuration of the administrator. Group Edit in the menu of the group tile. Workflow The workflow panel of the editor (select no node).

Names use upper-case letters, digits and _ (DATABASE_SERVER). The prefix PIPE_ is reserved. An empty value means "not set here".

docs.title: Which value applies
docs.text:
For the active environment, say PROD:

  1. a PROD value on the workflow, the group or the instance, the lowest level first;
  2. otherwise a DEFAULT value on the workflow, the group or the instance, the lowest level first.

So a PROD value of the instance wins over a DEFAULT value of the workflow. Overriding a value per environment needs a value for that environment.

Example: the instance has DATABASE_SERVER = db-test for DEFAULT and db-prod for PROD. Workflows running in PROD get db-prod, all others db-test.

docs.title: Using variables
docs.text:
• In expressions: {{ $vars.DATABASE_SERVER }}. {{ $environment }} is the environment of the run. Reading a variable that isn't defined stops the node with an error that names the variable and the environment.
  • In scripts: Run Script, Run Scripts Folder and Run Scripts Repo get all variables as environment variables, plus PIPE_ENVIRONMENT. The Environment variables of the node override them.

docs.title: Secret variables
docs.text: The lock next to the name marks a variable as secret. Its values are stored encrypted, shown as password fields and replaced by *** in logs, error messages and script output. Passwords and keys still belong in credentials where a node supports one.

docs.title: Running in another environment
docs.text:
• Run in the editor: the field next to the button chooses the environment of manual runs. It starts at the effective environment, marked (saved). Another choice is outlined in its color and applies only to runs from the editor; it isn't saved.
  • Schedules (Cron Trigger) always run in the effective environment.
  • Webhooks run in the effective environment. A caller may choose another one with the header X-Pipe-Environment: TEST, but only one listed under Webhook callers may choose in the workflow panel. Any other gets 400, see Triggers and webhooks.
  • Sub-workflows and error workflows run in the environment of the run that started them, so a test run never reaches production data through Execute Workflow.

Each execution records its environment. The executions list of the workflow shows it and can filter by it.

Inputs: main · Outputs: main

Parameter Type Description Messagemessage JSON Supports expressions. Levellevel one of: trace, debug, information, warning, error, critical, none Default: information.

docs.title: No Operation
docs.text:
Passes items through unchanged.

Inputs: main · Outputs: main

This node has no parameters.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Defines what a user sees in the portal at the end of the run: text, Markdown or a table. Without a Result node the portal shows only the status. Outputs one item with the result, so place it at the end of the workflow.

Inputs: main · Outputs: main

Parameter Type Description Kindkind one of: text, markdown, table Text and Markdown show the content; Table shows the incoming items, one row per item. Default: text. Titletitle text Supports expressions. Contentcontent text For Text and Markdown; evaluated for the first incoming item. Supports expressions. Error messageerrorMessage text Shown to the portal user when the run fails. Without it the user sees a general message and the number of the run; details of errors stay with the admins. Supports expressions.

docs.title: gView.Pipe
docs.text: gView.Pipe ist eine Workflow-Anwendung: Im Editor verbindest du Nodes, und Items fließen von Node zu Node. Ein Workflow startet nach Zeitplan, über einen Webhook oder von Hand.

docs.title: Wo anfangen
docs.text:
• Anwenderhandbuch: Workflows bauen, ausführen und überwachen.
  • Administratorhandbuch: gView.Pipe installieren, konfigurieren und betreiben.
  • Entwicklerhandbuch: eigene Nodes als Plugins schreiben (nur auf Englisch).

docs.title: Administratorhandbuch
docs.text:
Dieses Handbuch richtet sich an Personen, die gView.Pipe installieren und betreiben.

  • Installation: ZIP und Docker, erster Start.
  • Konfiguration: Einstellungen, Ordner, Umgebungsvariablen.
  • Anmeldung: Anmeldung mit festen Benutzern oder einem Identity Provider (OIDC).
  • Plugins: welche Plugins es gibt und wie man sie installiert.
  • Skripte ausführen: Skriptordner und Git-Server freigeben.
  • Betrieb: Reverse Proxy, Webhooks, Backup, Updates, Logs.
  • Sicherheit: was die App schützt und was du schützen musst.
  • Fehlersuche: typische Probleme und ihre Ursachen.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text: Skripte und CI-Pipelines nutzen die REST API unter /api/v1, um Workflows auszuführen, Executions abzufragen und Workflows zu deployen. Die API hat eigene Schlüssel; die Anmeldung der UI nutzt sie nie.

docs.title: API-Schlüssel
docs.text:
Schlüssel legst du auf der Seite API keys an (Navigation). Ein Schlüssel hat:

Einstellung Bedeutung Name Wer oder was ihn nutzt, z. B. CI Deploy. Mit dem Schlüssel gestartete Läufe zeigen in der Historie API · CI Deploy. Rights Read: Workflows, Executions, Gruppen. Run: Läufe starten, stoppen, wiederholen. Deploy: Workflows anlegen, ändern, löschen, aktivieren. Portal: nur die Portal-Endpunkte für das Anwender-Portal; allein verwenden. Only these groups Beschränkt den Schlüssel auf die Workflows dieser Gruppen. Andere Workflows sieht er gar nicht, auch keine ohne Gruppe. Expires Nach diesem Tag wird der Schlüssel abgelehnt. Leer: nie.

Der Schlüssel (pipe_…) wird einmal angezeigt, beim Anlegen. Gespeichert wird nur sein SHA-256 (data/api-keys.json); ein verlorener Schlüssel lässt sich also nicht mehr anzeigen: Lösche ihn und lege einen neuen an. Am Präfix pipe_ erkennen Secret-Scanner, z. B. von GitHub, versehentlich eingecheckte Schlüssel.

Schicke den Schlüssel als Header:

X-Pipe-Api-Key: pipe_…

oder als Authorization: Bearer pipe_….

Warning

Nur Benutzer mit der Rolle admin können Schlüssel anlegen. Mit Pipe:Auth:Mode none ist jeder admin, der die UI erreicht. Schütze die UI mit einer Anmeldung, bevor du dich auf Schlüssel verlässt. Mehr als 60 Fehlversuche pro Minute von einer Adresse werden mit 429 beantwortet.

docs.title: Endpunkte
docs.text:
Die API ist in /api/v1/openapi.json (OpenAPI 3) beschrieben. Lade die Datei in ein Werkzeug deiner Wahl, z. B. Postman, Bruno oder einen OpenAPI-Viewer, um die Endpunkte auszuprobieren.

Methode und Pfad Recht Macht GET /api/v1/workflows read Listet die Workflows. GET /api/v1/workflows/{id} read Der Workflow als JSON, mit seiner Version als ETag. PUT /api/v1/workflows/{id} deploy Legt den Workflow an oder ersetzt ihn (siehe unten). DELETE /api/v1/workflows/{id} deploy Löscht den Workflow. POST /api/v1/workflows/{id}/activate, /deactivate deploy Schaltet seine Trigger ein oder aus. POST /api/v1/workflows/{id}/run run Startet einen Lauf (siehe unten). GET /api/v1/executions read Executions, die neueste zuerst. Filter: workflowId, status, mode, from, before, limit. GET /api/v1/executions/{workflowId}/{id} read Eine Execution mit Eingabe, Ausgabe und Logs jedes Nodes. POST /api/v1/executions/{workflowId}/{id}/cancel run Stoppt einen laufenden oder wartenden Lauf. POST /api/v1/executions/{workflowId}/{id}/replay run Führt die Execution erneut aus; Body { "fromNodeId": "…" }, um an einem Node zu beginnen (Replay). GET /api/v1/groups read Listet die Workflow-Gruppen. GET /api/v1/audit read Das Audit-Log, die neuesten zuerst. Filter: from, before, actor, area, objectId, limit. Nur für Schlüssel ohne Gruppen-Beschränkung.

Fehler werden als application/problem+json beantwortet, mit einem title, der sagt, was nicht stimmt.

docs.title: Einen Workflow ausführen
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/workflows/{id}/run
{ "items": [ { "name": "Ada" } ], "environment": "TEST", "wait": true, "timeoutSeconds": 30 }

Alle Felder sind optional. Der Lauf startet an allen Nodes ohne eingehende Verbindung, mit items als deren Eingabe (Vorgabe: ein leeres Item). Er verhält sich wie ein getriggerter Lauf: Angeheftete Daten werden ignoriert, der Fehler-Workflow startet bei einem Fehler, und die Warteschlange des Workflows gilt (Max queued runs).

Antwort Wann 200 { executionId, status, error, errorNode, node, items } wait und der Lauf endete rechtzeitig; items ist die Ausgabe des zuletzt beendeten Nodes. Auch ein fehlgeschlagener Lauf ist 200, mit status: "error". 202 { executionId, status } Ohne wait, oder der Lauf dauert länger als timeoutSeconds; frag später GET /executions/{workflowId}/{executionId}. 429 Der Workflow läuft schon, und seine Warteschlange ist voll.

docs.title: Einen Workflow deployen
docs.text:
PUT /api/v1/workflows/{id} nimmt das JSON eines Workflows, wie GET es liefert oder wie es in data/workflows liegt. Vor dem Speichern wird geprüft: eindeutige Node-Ids und -Namen, Verbindungen zwischen vorhandenen Nodes, keine Zyklen, installierte Node-Typen, gültige Parameter. Probleme werden mit 422 und einer Liste in details.errors beantwortet. Credentials, die es auf diesem Server nicht gibt, stehen als details.warnings in der Antwort, sind aber keine Fehler.

Schicke If-Match mit dem ETag eines GET, um sicherzugehen, dass niemand den Workflow zwischendurch geändert hat; sonst bekommst du 412. Ohne If-Match wird der Workflow ersetzt. Ist der Workflow aktiv, werden seine Trigger mit der neuen Version neu geladen.

docs.title: Beispiele
docs.text:
curlPowerShell 
KEY=pipe_...
# ausführen und auf das Ergebnis warten
curl -s -X POST https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/workflows/hello-pipe/run \
  -H "X-Pipe-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "items": [ { "name": "Ada" } ], "wait": true }'

# einen Workflow aus einer Datei deployen
curl -s -X PUT https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/workflows/hello-pipe \
  -H "X-Pipe-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary @hello-pipe.json

# die letzten fehlgeschlagenen Läufe
curl -s "https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/executions?status=error&limit=10" -H "X-Pipe-Api-Key: $KEY"

$headers = @{ "X-Pipe-Api-Key" = "pipe_..." }
# ausführen und auf das Ergebnis warten
$body = @{ items = @(@{ name = "Ada" }); wait = $true } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/workflows/hello-pipe/run `
  -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body

# einen Workflow aus einer Datei deployen
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Put -Uri https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/workflows/hello-pipe `
  -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/json" -InFile hello-pipe.json

# die letzten fehlgeschlagenen Läufe
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://pipe.example.com/api/v1/executions?status=error&limit=10" -Headers $headers

Credentials, Variablen und Gruppen lassen sich über die API nicht ändern; richte sie in der UI ein.

docs.title: Portal-Endpunkte
docs.text:
Für das Anwender-Portal (Anwender, die Workflows ausführen, aber nicht bearbeiten) erreicht ein Key mit dem Recht Portal nur /api/v1/portal. Er kann nichts anderes, und kein anderer Key erreicht diese Endpunkte. Jede Anfrage nennt den Anwender, für den sie gilt, im Header X-Pipe-On-Behalf-Of und kann die Portal-Rollen des Anwenders in X-Pipe-On-Behalf-Of-Roles auflisten (jede Rolle prozentcodiert, durch Kommas getrennt); Läufe zeigen portal:<Anwender> als Starter, und Anwender sehen und stoppen nur ihre eigenen Läufe. Der Portal-Server wird darin als vertrauenswürdig behandelt, dass er den richtigen Anwender nennt. Halte den Key deshalb auf diesem Server und lass nur ihn das Backend erreichen.

Methode und Pfad Macht GET /api/v1/portal/workflows Die veröffentlichten Workflows mit Kategorie, Formular und Einstellungen zum Lauf. POST /api/v1/portal/workflows/{id}/run Startet einen Lauf. Body { "values": { … }, "mode": "wait" oder "background" }. Die Werte werden gegen das Formular geprüft (422 mit den falschen Feldern). Beim Warten kommt das Ergebnis zurück, oder 202, wenn das Warte-Timeout abgelaufen ist. GET /api/v1/portal/executions Die Läufe des Anwenders, neueste zuerst, auch die laufenden. GET /api/v1/portal/executions/{workflowId}/{id} Status und Ergebnis eines Laufs des Anwenders. POST /api/v1/portal/executions/{workflowId}/{id}/cancel Stoppt einen Lauf des Anwenders, falls der Workflow das nicht verbietet.

Welche Workflows erscheinen, stellst du in den Workflow-Einstellungen ein: Sichtbar sind nur Workflows mit Publish in portal, in der Kategorie ihrer Gruppe. Der Form Trigger legt das Formular fest, der Result-Node, was der Anwender am Ende sieht. Anwender sehen nie rohe Items oder Fehlerdetails der Nodes: Ein fehlgeschlagener Lauf zeigt die Error message des Result-Nodes oder einen allgemeinen Text mit der Nummer des Laufs.

Jedes Feld des Formulars hat einen Namen, einen Typ (Text, mehrzeiliger Text, Zahl, Ja/Nein, Datum, Auswahl, Passwort), ein Label, eine Beschreibung, einen Platzhalter, einen Standardwert und Required. Textfelder können ein Muster haben, einen regulären Ausdruck, auf den der Text als Ganzes passen muss (z. B. [A-Z]{1,2}-\d{1,5}), mit der Meldung, die sonst erscheint. Das Portal kann es schon beim Tippen prüfen; das Backend prüft es bei jedem Start nochmal. Beschränke Muster auf das, was .NET und JavaScript gemeinsam verstehen.

Einstellungen des Backends für das Portal (Abschnitt Pipe:Portal):

Einstellung Bedeutung MaxRunsPerUser Läufe, die ein Anwender gleichzeitig haben darf (Standard 3, 0 = unbegrenzt); weitere werden mit 429 beantwortet. HistoryDays Tage, die Ergebnis und eingegebene Werte eines Laufs für den Anwender aufbewahrt werden (Standard 30, 0 = immer); danach wird nur noch der Status gezeigt. NotifyWorkflowId Der Workflow, der die Mail bei Fertigstellung sendet. Ohne ihn bietet das Portal keine Mail an. PublicUrl Die Adresse des Portals, für den Link in dieser Mail.

GET /api/v1/portal/info sagt dem Portal, ob eine Mail gesendet werden kann (mailWhenDone), und die aufbewahrten Tage (historyDays). notifyEmail im Body eines Laufs verlangt die Mail.

docs.title: Anmeldung
docs.text:
gView.Pipe kennt drei Anmeldemodi. Du wählst einen pro Instanz in _config/auth.config:

Modus Bedeutung none Keine Anmeldung (Vorgabe). Jeder, der die Adresse erreicht, darf die App benutzen. Nur auf localhost oder in einem geschützten Netz verwenden. forms Ein Anmeldeformular mit Benutzern aus der Konfiguration. oidc Anmeldung bei einem Identity Provider mit OpenID Connect, zum Beispiel IdentityServer.NET.

Die Anmeldung schützt die Oberfläche. Webhooks und die Dokumentation unter /docs bleiben ohne Anmeldung erreichbar; schütze Webhooks mit einem Credential (siehe Sicherheit). Wer angemeldet ist, darf alles.

docs.title: Die Datei auth.config
docs.text:
Beim ersten Start legt die App _config/auth.config aus der Vorlage _setup/proto/auth.config an, neben pipe.config (siehe Konfiguration). Umgebungsvariablen überschreiben sie, zum Beispiel Pipe__Auth__Mode=forms.

Einstellung Vorgabe Bedeutung Pipe:Auth:Mode none none, forms oder oidc. Pipe:Auth:SessionMinutes 480 Minuten ohne Anfrage, bis die Anmeldung abläuft. Jede Anfrage verlängert sie. Pipe:Auth:UseForwardedHeaders false Den Headern X-Forwarded-For/-Proto/-Host eines Reverse Proxys vertrauen. Nötig für OIDC hinter einem Proxy, der https beendet. Pipe:Auth:Users Benutzer des Modus forms, siehe unten. Pipe:Auth:LoginAttemptsPerMinute 10 Anmeldeversuche pro Minute und Client-Adresse; weitere werden mit 429 beantwortet. Pipe:Auth:Oidc:* Einstellungen des Modus oidc, siehe unten.

docs.title: Forms: feste Benutzer
docs.text:
{
  "Pipe": {
    "Auth": {
      "Mode": "forms",
      "Users": [
        { "Name": "admin", "PasswordHash": "pbkdf2-sha256$210000$..." },
        { "Name": "editor", "Password": "Klartext" }
      ]
    }
  }
}

  • PasswordHash ist vorzuziehen. Du erzeugst ihn mit der App selbst:

    dotnet gView.Pipe.Shell.dll --hash-password "mein Passwort"

  • Password im Klartext geht auch, schreibt aber bei jedem Start eine Warnung ins Log. Sind beide gesetzt, zählt der Hash.

  • Email (optional) ist die Adresse für Mails an den Benutzer, z. B. wenn ein Lauf des Portals fertig ist.
  • Bei Benutzernamen spielt Groß-/Kleinschreibung keine Rolle.
  • Nach einem falschen Passwort wartet die App eine Sekunde; die Zahl der Versuche pro Adresse ist begrenzt.

docs.title: Docker: das Admin-Passwort als Variable
docs.text:
docker run -d --name gview-pipe -p 8080:8080 \
  -v gview-pipe-data:/app/data \
  -e PIPE_ADMIN_PASSWORD=change-me \
  ghcr.io/jugstalt/gview-pipe:latest

PIPE_ADMIN_PASSWORD setzt das Passwort des Benutzers admin (einen anderen Namen mit PIPE_ADMIN_USER). Es ersetzt diesen Benutzer aus auth.config, behält die übrigen und schaltet den Modus none auf forms.

docs.title: OIDC: Identity Provider
docs.text:
{
  "Pipe": {
    "Auth": {
      "Mode": "oidc",
      "Oidc": {
        "Authority": "https://login.example.com",
        "ClientId": "gview-pipe",
        "ClientSecret": "secret",
        "Scopes": [ "openid", "profile", "role" ],
        "RoleClaimType": "role",
        "NameClaimType": "name",
        "RequiredRoles": [ "gview-pipe" ]
      }
    }
  }
}
Einstellung Vorgabe Bedeutung Authority Adresse des Identity Providers. Pflicht. ClientId Client-Id beim Provider. Pflicht. ClientSecret Secret des Clients; für einen öffentlichen Client leer lassen. In Docker: Pipe__Auth__Oidc__ClientSecret. Scopes openid profile role Angeforderte Scopes. RoleClaimType role Claim mit den Rollen des Benutzers. NameClaimType name Claim, der als Benutzername angezeigt wird. RequiredRoles (leer) Der Benutzer braucht eine dieser Rollen. Leer: Jeder Benutzer des Providers darf hinein. RequireHttpsMetadata true Nur für einen Test-Provider ohne https auf false setzen.

Die App verwendet den Authorization Code Flow mit PKCE. Trage beim Provider ein:

  • die Redirect-URI https://<app>/signin-oidc,
  • die Post-Logout-Redirect-URI https://<app>/signout-callback-oidc.

Ein Benutzer ohne eine der verlangten Rollen sieht eine Seite No access mit einem Button Sign out. Die Abmeldung beendet auch die Sitzung beim Provider, damit sich ein anderes Konto anmelden kann.

Hinter einem Reverse Proxy, der https beendet, setze UseForwardedHeaders auf true, sonst beginnen die Redirect-URIs mit http:// (siehe Betrieb).

docs.title: Testen mit dem IdentityServer.NET des AppHost
docs.text:
Der AppHost startet IdentityServer.NET unter https://localhost:8443 (ADD_IDENTITYSERVER, Admin admin@is.net mit dem Passwort admin) mit dem Client local-gview-pipe/secret für https://localhost:7240. Windows muss seinem selbstsignierten Zertifikat vertrauen (in die vertrauenswürdigen Stammzertifikate des Benutzers importieren), sonst lehnen Browser und App es ab. In seiner Admin-Oberfläche (https://localhost:8443/admin):

  1. Lege die Rolle gview-pipe an (Roles).
  2. Lege einen Benutzer mit dieser Rolle und einen ohne an (Users, dann User Roles).
  3. Setze Mode in _config/auth.config auf oidc; die Vorlage enthält die Einstellungen dieses Clients schon.

Der Benutzer mit der Rolle kann arbeiten, der andere sieht No access.

Der AppHost legt dafür schon Benutzer an (Passwort in Klammern), alle mit der Rolle gview-pipe: pipe-viewer@is.net (viewer), pipe-operator@is.net (operator), pipe-editor@is.net (editor) und pipe-admin@is.net (admin) sowie pipe-samples@is.net (samples), der allgemein viewer und nur in der Gruppe Samples editor ist. Er bildet ihre Rollen (pipe-viewers, pipe-operators, pipe-editors, pipe-admins und pipe-samples-editors als editor@samples) auf die Rollen der Shell ab; du schaltest den Modus also nur noch ein: Aktiviere #define PIPE_OIDC oben in AppHost.cs (es setzt Mode, den Provider und den Client für dich, und ein Benutzer braucht die Rolle gview-pipe). Mit #define PIPE_FORMS hat die Shell stattdessen feste Benutzer ohne IdentityServer: viewer, operator, editor, admin und samples, jeweils mit dem Namen als Passwort. Es darf nur eines von beiden definiert sein. Die Einstellungen kommen als Umgebungsvariablen in die Shell und gelten damit vor _config/auth.config; Listen wie Users werden nach Position zusammengeführt, schiebe also eine eigene _config/auth.config mit Benutzern beiseite. Der Benutzer portal@is.net (portal) mit der Rolle portal-demo ist für das Portal.

docs.title: Rollen
docs.text:
Mit Anmeldung hat jeder Benutzer eine Rolle. Jede Rolle darf, was die vorherigen dürfen:

Rolle Darf viewer Workflows, Executions und Gruppen sehen operator Workflows ausführen, stoppen und wiederholen; aktivieren und deaktivieren editor Workflows und Gruppen anlegen, ändern und löschen; Pin Data admin Credentials, die Variablen der Instanz, API-Schlüssel

viewer und operator öffnen Workflows nur lesend: Der Editor zeigt Read only, ohne Palette und Save; die Felder lassen sich nicht ändern. Seiten und Knöpfe, die eine Rolle nicht nutzen darf, sind ausgeblendet oder deaktiviert. Ohne Anmeldung (Mode none) ist jeder admin.

Ein Benutzer kann für die Workflows einer Gruppe eine andere Rolle haben, z. B. allgemein viewer, aber editor in der Gruppe Billing. Credentials, Instanz-Variablen und API-Schlüssel richten sich nur nach der Rolle für die Instanz. Gruppen werden über ihre Id angegeben (billing), wie sie in der Adresse der Gruppenseite steht.

Forms: pro Benutzer in auth.config:

"Users": [
  { "Name": "admin", "PasswordHash": "…", "Role": "admin" },
  { "Name": "ada", "PasswordHash": "…", "Role": "viewer", "GroupRoles": { "billing": "editor" } }
]

OIDC: Bilde Werte des Rollen-Claims (RoleClaimType) auf Rollen ab; rolle@gruppe gibt die Rolle für eine Gruppe. Der höchste Treffer gilt, und eine Gruppe bekommt nie weniger als die Rolle für die Instanz:

"Oidc": {
  "RoleMappings": {
    "pipe-admins": "admin",
    "pipe-operators": "operator",
    "pipe-billing": "editor@billing"
  }
}

Benutzer ohne Rolle (ein Forms-Benutzer ohne Role, ein OIDC-Benutzer ohne abgebildeten Claim) bekommen DefaultRole. Die Vorgabe ist admin, damit eine Installation von vor den Rollen wie bisher funktioniert. Sobald du die Rollen vergeben hast, stelle sie auf viewer:

"DefaultRole": "viewer"

Die Rollen werden bei jeder Prüfung aus der Konfiguration ermittelt und nicht in der Anmeldung gespeichert: Nach einer Änderung an auth.config und einem Neustart der App gelten sie ohne erneute Anmeldung. Das Konto-Menü zeigt die eigene Rolle und mit (+ groups), dass es in manchen Gruppen andere gibt.

docs.title: Abmelden
docs.text: Mit Anmeldung zeigt das Konto-Symbol oben rechts den Benutzernamen, die Rolle und Sign out.

docs.title: Kommandozeile
docs.text: gview-gview-pipe ist ein Kommandozeilen-Client der REST API für Skripte und CI-Pipelines: Workflows aus Dateien bereitstellen, Läufe starten und auf sie warten, Ausführungen ansehen.

docs.title: Installieren
docs.text:
dotnet tool install --global gView.Pipe.Cli
gview-pipe --help

Das geht, sobald das Paket auf NuGet veröffentlicht ist. Bis dahin baust du es aus dem Quellcode und installierst es aus dem Ordner:

dotnet pack src/gView.Pipe.Cli -c Release -o artifacts/cli
dotnet tool install --global gView.Pipe.Cli --add-source artifacts/cli

Nach einer Änderung packst du neu und rufst dotnet tool update --global gView.Pipe.Cli --add-source artifacts/cli auf (erhöhe vorher die Version in Directory.Build.props, sonst wird das zwischengespeicherte Paket verwendet). dotnet tool uninstall --global gView.Pipe.Cli entfernt es.

Es braucht die .NET-10-Runtime und einen API-Schlüssel mit den Rechten für das, was du tust (read, run, deploy).

docs.title: Verbinden
docs.text:
Setze die Adresse des Servers und den Schlüssel als Umgebungsvariablen, damit der Schlüssel weder in der Prozessliste noch in den Logs der Pipeline erscheint:

bashPowerShell 
export PIPE_URL=https://pipe.example.com
export PIPE_API_KEY=pipe_...

$env:PIPE_URL = "https://pipe.example.com"
$env:PIPE_API_KEY = "pipe_..."

--url und --key tun dasselbe für einen Aufruf.

docs.title: Befehle
docs.text: Befehl Tut gview-pipe workflows list [--json] Listet die Workflows. gview-pipe workflows get <id> Gibt den Workflow als JSON aus. gview-pipe workflows export <id> --out <Datei oder Ordner> Speichert den Workflow als Datei; bei einem Ordner heißt sie <id>.json. gview-pipe workflows deploy <Datei oder Ordner>... [--dry-run] [--force] Legt Workflows aus JSON-Dateien an oder ersetzt sie (Ordner: alle *.json darunter). gview-pipe workflows delete <id> Löscht einen Workflow. gview-pipe workflows activate <id>, deactivate <id> Schaltet seine Trigger ein oder aus. gview-pipe run <id> [--wait] [--input <Datei oder ->] [--environment <Name>] [--timeout <Sekunden>] [--json] Startet einen Lauf. gview-pipe executions list [--workflow <id>] [--status <Status>] [--limit <n>] [--json] Listet Ausführungen, neueste zuerst. gview-pipe executions get <workflowId> <id> Eine Ausführung mit ihren Node-Läufen. gview-pipe executions cancel <workflowId> <id> Stoppt einen laufenden oder wartenden Lauf. gview-pipe executions replay <workflowId> <id> [--from <nodeId>] Führt eine Ausführung erneut aus.

docs.title: Bereitstellen
docs.text:
gview-pipe workflows deploy workflows/            # jede *.json unter dem Ordner
gview-pipe workflows deploy hello-pipe.json --dry-run

Die Datei ist das JSON eines Workflows, wie es gview-pipe workflows export schreibt oder wie es in data/workflows liegt; die id darin benennt den Workflow. Der Server prüft ihn vor dem Speichern; Probleme werden aufgelistet, und der Exit-Code ist 2.

  • Ein vorhandener Workflow wird nur ersetzt, wenn ihn seit dem Lesen durch den Befehl niemand geändert hat, zum Beispiel im Editor. Sonst bricht der Befehl mit einer Meldung ab; --force ersetzt ihn trotzdem.
  • --dry-run meldet nur would create oder would update. Er prüft den Workflow nicht; das macht der Server beim echten Deploy.
  • deploy löscht nie. Entferne Workflows einzeln mit gview-pipe workflows delete.
  • Credentials, die es auf dem Server nicht gibt, werden als Warnungen gemeldet.

docs.title: Ausführen
docs.text:
gview-pipe run hello-pipe                                   # startet ihn, gibt die Execution-Id aus
gview-pipe run hello-pipe --wait --input item.json          # wartet und gibt die Items des letzten Nodes aus
echo '{ "name": "Ada" }' | gview-pipe run hello-pipe --wait --input -

--input ist ein JSON-Objekt (ein Item) oder ein Array von Objekten; - liest es von der Standardeingabe. Der Lauf startet wie ein getriggerter Lauf, siehe Einen Workflow ausführen.

docs.title: Exit-Codes
docs.text:
Code Bedeutung 0 Erledigt. Ohne --wait gilt ein gestarteter Lauf als erledigt. 1 gview-pipe run --wait: Der Lauf endete mit dem Status error. 2 Falscher Aufruf, oder der Server hat ihn abgelehnt (401 Schlüssel, 404, 422 ungültiger Workflow, 429 Warteschlange voll).

Ein Pipeline-Schritt kann den Befehl deshalb direkt verwenden: Ein fehlgeschlagener Lauf oder ein abgelehntes Deploy lässt den Schritt fehlschlagen.

# Beispiel: GitHub Actions
- run: dotnet tool install --global gView.Pipe.Cli
- run: gview-pipe workflows deploy workflows/
  env:
    PIPE_URL: ${{ vars.PIPE_URL }}
    PIPE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PIPE_API_KEY }}

docs.title: Konfiguration
docs.text:
Die Einstellungen stehen in _config/pipe.config im Arbeitsordner der App (im Abschnitt Pipe, JSON mit Kommentaren). Fehlt die Datei beim Start, legt die App sie aus der Vorlage _setup/proto/pipe.config an; danach passt du sie an. appsettings.json enthält nur ASP.NET-Core-Einstellungen wie Logging. Umgebungsvariablen und die Kommandozeile überschreiben pipe.config. Die Startskripte im ZIP setzen die Ordner als Umgebungsvariablen.

Die Anmeldung hat eine eigene Datei _config/auth.config, die genauso aus _setup/proto/auth.config entsteht (siehe Anmeldung).

Im Docker-Image ist /app/_config ein Volume, damit die Dateien Updates überstehen.

docs.title: Konfiguration über Updates behalten
docs.text: Die Variable PIPE_CONFIG_PATH verlegt den Ordner _config. Die Startskripte und gview-pipe-service.bat install setzen sie auf <root>\_config, neben die Versionsordner. So hat jede Installation (jeder Root-Ordner) ihre eigene pipe.config und behält sie über Updates. Beim ersten Start legt die App sie dort aus der Vorlage an. Bearbeite <root>\_config\pipe.config; der Versionsordner hat kein eigenes _config.

docs.title: Einstellungen
Environments und Variablen
docs.text:
Jede Instanz läuft in einem Environment: ein Testserver in TEST, der Produktionsserver in PROD. Gruppen und Workflows erben es, wenn sie kein eigenes setzen, siehe Variablen und Environments. Anwender können das Environment der Instanz in der App nicht ändern.

{
  "Pipe": {
    "Environment": "PROD",
    "Environments": [ "TEST", "STAGE", "PROD" ],
    "Variables": {
      "DATABASE_SERVER": { "DEFAULT": "db-test", "PROD": "db-prod" },
      "DATABASE_PASSWORD": { "PROD": "..." }
    },
    "SecretVariables": [ "DATABASE_PASSWORD" ]
  }
}

Variablen der Konfiguration sind die unterste Ebene. Werte, die auf der Seite Variables der App eingetragen werden, gewinnen je Environment gegen sie. Die App speichert sie in variables.json im Datenordner; geheime Werte werden mit den Schlüsseln in keys/ verschlüsselt. Geheime Werte von Gruppen und Workflows werden genauso verschlüsselt, eine Workflow-Datei, die in eine andere Installation kopiert wird, verliert sie also.

docs.title: Umgebungsvariablen
docs.text:
Für die Verschachtelung nimmst du zwei Unterstriche:

Pipe__DataPath=/var/lib/gview-pipe/data
Pipe__FileRoots__import=/srv/import
Pipe__Scripts__ScriptRoots__scripts=/srv/scripts
Pipe__Scripts__GitServers__company__Url=https://git.example.com
Pipe__Environment=PROD
Pipe__Variables__DATABASE_SERVER__PROD=db-prod

docs.title: Lauschadresse
docs.text:
Die Startskripte lauschen standardmäßig auf http://localhost:5100. Um das zu ändern, etwa für eine zweite Instanz auf demselben Rechner, setze urls oben in pipe.config (neben Pipe, nicht darin):

{
  "urls": "http://localhost:5101",
  "Pipe": { ... }
}

urls in pipe.config gewinnt gegen ASPNETCORE_URLS; --urls auf der Kommandozeile gewinnt gegen beide. Der Windows-Dienst übergibt seinen Port mit --urls (gview-pipe-service.bat install <name> <port>). Das Docker-Image nutzt http://*:8080.

docs.title: Grenzen, die nicht in der Konfiguration stehen
docs.text:
Einige Optionen lassen sich nur im Code setzen (Program.cs des Shell), zum Beispiel wie lange ein Wait-Node höchstens wartet (eine Stunde), die JavaScript-Grenzen und die maximale Body-Größe eines Webhooks (10 MB). Frag deinen Entwickler, wenn du sie ändern willst.

Pro Workflow stellst du die maximale Zahl gleichzeitiger Läufe (Vorgabe 1) im Workflow-Panel des Editors ein. Weitere gleichzeitige Läufe werden übersprungen, und ein Webhook-Aufrufer bekommt 429, sofern Max queued runs getriggerte Läufe nicht warten lässt.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: gView.Pipe braucht die .NET-10-Runtime (ASP.NET Core). Das Docker-Image bringt sie mit.

docs.title: ZIP (Windows und Linux)
docs.text:
Lade gview-pipe-win64-<Version>.zip oder gview-pipe-linux64-<Version>.zip herunter und entpacke sie in einen Ordner deiner Wahl, zum Beispiel C:\gview-pipe. Das ZIP enthält je Version einen Ordner:

gview-pipe\
  0.1.0\
    pipe\                 die App und ihre Plugins
    gview-pipe.bat        Startskript (unter Linux gview-pipe.sh)
  data\                   wird beim ersten Start angelegt: Workflows, Executions, Credentials, Schlüssel
  files\                  Ordner für Read File / Write File
  scripts\                Ordner für Run Script

data, files und scripts liegen neben den Versionsordnern und überstehen deshalb ein Update. Das Startskript setzt ihren Ort für dich.

Starte die App mit dem Startskript. Sie lauscht auf http://localhost:5100. Öffne diese Adresse im Browser.

Note

Das Startskript bindet nur an localhost. Damit andere Rechner die App erreichen, setze einen Reverse Proxy davor (siehe Betrieb) oder setze urls in <root>\_config\pipe.config (siehe Konfiguration). Standardmäßig gibt es keine Anmeldung: Schalte eine ein, bevor andere die App erreichen (siehe Anmeldung).

Beim ersten Start mit leerem Ordner data kopiert gView.Pipe die Beispiel-Workflows in die Gruppe Samples.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
docker run -d --name gview-pipe -p 8080:8080 \
  -v gview-pipe-data:/app/data \
  ghcr.io/jugstalt/gview-pipe:latest
  • Die App lauscht im Container auf Port 8080.
  • /app/data enthält den gesamten Laufzeitzustand: Binde ein Volume oder einen Ordner ein, sonst gehen die Daten mit dem Container verloren.
  • Das Image enthält git (für Run Scripts Repo) und python3 (für .py-Skripte). Es hat weder PowerShell noch eine Windows-Shell, also laufen .ps1-, .bat- und .cmd-Skripte darin nicht.
  • Für Read File / Write File und Skriptordner bindest du die Ordner ein und nennst sie in der Konfiguration, zum Beispiel -v /srv/pipe/files:/app/files -v /srv/pipe/scripts:/app/scripts. Die Vorgaben sind files und scripts unterhalb von /app.
  • Für eine Anmeldung mit dem Benutzer admin ergänze -e PIPE_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<Passwort> (siehe Anmeldung).

Einstellungen übergibst du als Umgebungsvariablen, siehe Konfiguration.

docs.title: Automatisch starten
docs.text:
Das Startskript lässt die App nur laufen, solange du angemeldet bist. Damit sie auf einem Server dauerhaft läuft, betreibe sie als Windows-Dienst, im IIS, als systemd-Unit oder in Docker. Starte sie in jedem Fall unter einem Konto mit eingeschränkten Rechten, denn Skripte laufen mit den Rechten dieses Kontos (siehe Sicherheit).

Aktive Workflows mit einem Cron- oder Webhook-Trigger werden beim Start der App wieder scharf geschaltet.

docs.title: Windows-Dienst
docs.text:
Im Versionsordner liegt gview-pipe-service.bat. Führe es in einer Eingabeaufforderung als Administrator aus:

gview-pipe-service.bat install [name] [port]
gview-pipe-service.bat uninstall [name]

install legt den Dienst an und startet ihn:

  • Dienstname gview-pipe, mit Namen gview-pipe-<name>. Er startet automatisch (verzögert) und wird nach einem Absturz neu gestartet.
  • Er lauscht auf http://localhost:<port> (Vorgabe 5100), wie das Startskript.
  • Er läuft unter dem virtuellen Konto NT SERVICE\gview-pipe[-<name>], das nur in data, files, scripts und _config schreiben darf.
  • data, files, scripts und _config neben den Versionsordnern werden als Umgebungsvariablen des Dienstes gesetzt, wie im Startskript.

Mehrere Instanzen auf einem Server, zum Beispiel Produktion und Test: Entpacke das ZIP je Instanz in einen eigenen Root-Ordner und gib jeder einen Namen und einen Port.

D:\gview-pipe-prod\0.1.0\gview-pipe-service.bat install prod 5100
D:\gview-pipe-test\0.1.0\gview-pipe-service.bat install test 5200

install verweigert einen Namen, dessen Dienst zu einem anderen Root-Ordner gehört.

Update: Entpacke die neue Version in denselben Root-Ordner und führe ihr gview-pipe-service.bat install mit demselben Namen und Port aus. Das Skript stoppt den Dienst, stellt ihn auf die neue Version um und startet ihn wieder. Zurück geht es mit install der alten Version.

Eigenes Konto: Für Netzwerkfreigaben oder Git mit Windows-Anmeldung reicht das virtuelle Konto nicht. Trage in den Diensteigenschaften (Reiter Anmelden) ein Domänen- oder lokales Konto ein und gib ihm Schreibrechte auf dieselben Ordner.

Das Log geht ins Windows-Ereignisprotokoll (Anwendungsprotokoll, Quelle gView.Pipe, Warnungen und Fehler).

docs.title: IIS
docs.text:
gView.Pipe läuft im IIS wie jede ASP.NET-Core-App:
